topics.h: Atoms are like guests at a wedding: everyone who walks in must walk out — just with new partners!
p: A chemical reaction makes new substances. Signs: change in colour, change in state, gas given off, change in temperature or a precipitate forming.
A word equation names the reactants (left) and products (right), joined by an arrow: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.
A skeletal equation uses formulae but may be unbalanced: Mg + O₂ → MgO.
Law of conservation of mass: mass is neither created nor destroyed, so each element must have the same number of atoms on both sides. We balance by changing coefficients, never the formulae.
State symbols show physical state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. Conditions such as heat or a catalyst are written above or below the arrow.

ex.q: Balance: Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂ (iron reacting with steam).
st: Count atoms: left Fe 1, H 2, O 1; right Fe 3, H 2, O 4.
Start with the compound having the most atoms, Fe₃O₄: it has 4 O, so put 4 in front of H₂O.
Now left has 8 H, so put 4 in front of H₂.
Right has 3 Fe, so put 3 in front of Fe.
Check: Fe 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 4 = 4. Add states: steam is (g).
ex.a: 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)

topics.rl: When a Diwali sparkler (always lit with an adult around) glows bright white, metal powders such as aluminium or magnesium in it are reacting with oxygen — a real chemical change you can write as an equation.

topics.h: Some reactions join things, some break them apart, and some are like a dance where partners swap!
p: Combination: two or more reactants form one product, e.g. CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (quicklime to slaked lime, with lots of heat).
Decomposition: one reactant breaks into simpler products using heat (thermal), light (photolytic) or electricity (electrolytic), e.g. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating.
Displacement: a more reactive element pushes a less reactive one out of its compound, e.g. Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
Double displacement: two compounds exchange ions; often an insoluble precipitate forms, e.g. Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ (white) + 2NaCl.
Exothermic reactions release heat (burning, respiration); endothermic reactions absorb energy (most decompositions, photosynthesis).

ex.q: Think it through: an iron nail is dipped in blue copper sulphate solution for 20 minutes. What do you see, and what type of reaction is it?
st: Iron is more reactive than copper.
So iron displaces copper from copper sulphate: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
Copper deposits on the nail as a brownish coat.
Iron sulphate solution is pale green, so the blue colour fades.
One element replaces another in a compound — a displacement reaction.
ex.a: The nail turns brownish and the blue solution fades towards pale green: a displacement reaction.

topics.rl: Whitewashing walls before festivals uses slaked lime. It slowly reacts with carbon dioxide in air to form a thin layer of calcium carbonate, which gives walls a shine after two or three days.

topics.h: Every time something gains oxygen, something else is losing it — oxidation and reduction always come as a pair!
p: Oxidation: a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen. Reduction: a substance loses oxygen or gains hydrogen.
When both happen in the same reaction it is a redox reaction, e.g. CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (CuO is reduced, H₂ is oxidised).
Heating copper powder in air: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. The brown surface turns black as copper is oxidised.
Corrosion: a metal is slowly attacked by air, moisture or acids. Iron rusts (reddish-brown), silver turns black and copper gets a green coat.
Rancidity: fats and oils in food get oxidised, changing smell and taste. Airtight containers, antioxidants and filling chip packets with nitrogen slow it down.

ex.q: Think it through: in ZnO + C → Zn + CO, which substance is oxidised and which is reduced?
st: Zinc oxide (ZnO) loses its oxygen and becomes Zn — loss of oxygen is reduction.
Carbon (C) gains oxygen and becomes CO — gain of oxygen is oxidation.
Both happen together, so this is a redox reaction.
ex.a: ZnO is reduced and C is oxidised; it is a redox reaction.

topics.rl: Chip packets puff up because they are filled with nitrogen instead of air, so the oil in the chips does not get oxidised and turn rancid.

topics.h: A purple dye from a tiny lichen can tell you whether your nimbu-pani is acidic — that's the magic of indicators!
p: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red; bases taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue. Litmus is a purple dye from lichens.
Synthetic indicators: phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base. Turmeric turns reddish-brown in a base.
Olfactory indicators change smell: the odour of onion, vanilla essence or clove oil cannot be detected in a basic solution.
In water, acids give H⁺ ions (as H₃O⁺) and bases give OH⁻ ions. Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis.
pH scale runs from 0 to 14: 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 basic. Lower pH means more H⁺ ions; strong acids give many H⁺ ions, weak acids give fewer.

ex.q: Think it through: a universal indicator shows pH 2 for liquid A and pH 5 for liquid B. Which is more acidic, and which has more H⁺ ions?
st: Both are below 7, so both are acidic.
Lower pH means higher hydrogen ion concentration.
pH 2 is lower than pH 5.
ex.a: Liquid A (pH 2) is more acidic and has more H⁺ ions.

topics.rl: Your mouth becomes acidic after eating sweets as bacteria break down sugar; tooth enamel starts to corrode when mouth pH falls below 5.5, so brushing after meals helps.

topics.t: Neutralisation and reactions of acids and bases
topics.h: When an acid meets a base they cancel each other's sting — and leave behind salt and water!
p: Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water, e.g. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Heat is released.
Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas. Hydrogen burns with a pop sound when a burning splinter is brought near.
Acid + metal carbonate or hydrogencarbonate → salt + carbon dioxide + water. CO₂ turns lime water milky.
Acid + metal oxide → salt + water, so metal oxides are basic. Some metals like zinc also react with sodium hydroxide to give hydrogen (forming sodium zincate).
Salts of a strong acid and strong base (NaCl) are neutral, pH 7; strong acid + weak base (NH₄Cl) gives acidic salts; strong base + weak acid (Na₂CO₃, CH₃COONa) gives basic salts.

ex.q: Think it through: a farmer's soil is too acidic for his crop. What might he add, and why?
st: Acidic soil has too many H⁺ ions.
A base neutralises an acid, forming salt and water.
So he can add a mild base such as quicklime, slaked lime or chalk (calcium carbonate).
ex.a: He adds a base such as slaked lime or chalk to neutralise the extra acid.

topics.rl: Milk of magnesia, a mild base (magnesium hydroxide), is used as an antacid to neutralise excess stomach acid during indigestion.

topics.t: Common salt and chemicals made from it
topics.h: From one humble packet of namak, industries make bleach, baking soda, washing soda and more!
p: Common salt (NaCl) comes from sea water by evaporation and from rock salt deposits (brown due to impurities).
Chlor-alkali process: electricity is passed through brine (concentrated NaCl solution): 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂. Chlorine forms at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, NaOH near the cathode.
Bleaching powder is made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O. It bleaches cotton and linen, disinfects drinking water and is an oxidising agent.

Baking soda (NaHCO₃) is a mild, non-corrosive base. On heating: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. Baking powder = baking soda + a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid; the CO₂ makes cakes and dhokla soft and fluffy.

Washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, used in glass, soap and paper industries and to remove permanent hardness of water. Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) forms when gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) is heated to 373 K; with water it sets back into hard gypsum.

ex.q: Think it through: why must Plaster of Paris be stored in a moisture-proof container?
st: Plaster of Paris is CaSO₄·½H₂O.
With water it changes into gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O, which is a hard solid mass.
Moisture from the air would slowly make it set in the bag.
ex.a: Because moisture would turn it into hard gypsum and it would become useless.

topics.rl: Doctors use Plaster of Paris to support fractured bones, and potters use it to make moulds and decorative idols — it sets quickly into a hard shape.

topics.h: Gold so thin you can see light through it, and a metal that melts in your palm — metals are full of surprises!
p: Metals are usually lustrous, hard, malleable (beaten into sheets), ductile (drawn into wires), sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity. Silver and copper are the best conductors.
Exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature; sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife; gallium and caesium melt on your palm.

Non-metals are usually dull, brittle and poor conductors; they are solids or gases, but bromine is a liquid. Iodine is lustrous, graphite conducts electricity and diamond is the hardest natural substance.
Metals form basic oxides (e.g. MgO), while non-metals form acidic oxides (e.g. SO₂, CO₂). Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric — they react with both acids and bases.
Very reactive metals like sodium and potassium catch fire in air, so they are stored under kerosene. Silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperature.

ex.q: Think it through: a shiny grey solid conducts electricity, but it is brittle and breaks when hammered. Is it a metal?
st: Conducting electricity alone is not enough — graphite (a non-metal) conducts too.
Metals are malleable; they flatten instead of shattering.
Iodine and graphite show that some non-metals can be lustrous or conducting.
ex.a: Probably not: being brittle points to a non-metal (like graphite), even though it conducts.

topics.rl: Copper wires carry electricity in your home, aluminium foil wraps your rotis, and copper-bottom vessels heat dal evenly — all thanks to metallic properties.

topics.h: Metals compete like players in a kabaddi match — the stronger one always pulls the other out!
p: Reactivity series (most to least reactive): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
With water: Na and K react violently with cold water; Ca reacts less violently; Mg reacts with hot water; Al, Zn and Fe react only with steam; Pb, Cu, Ag and Au do not react.

Metals above hydrogen give hydrogen gas with dilute HCl. Nitric acid is an oxidising agent, so it usually does not give hydrogen (except Mg and Mn with very dilute HNO₃). Aqua regia (3 parts conc. HCl : 1 part conc. HNO₃) dissolves even gold.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain them, forming ionic compounds such as NaCl (Na: 2,8,1 → Na⁺; Cl: 2,8,7 → Cl⁻). Ionic compounds are hard, brittle solids with high melting points, dissolve in water but not in kerosene, and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved, not as solids.

ex.q: Think it through: why do calcium pieces start floating in water a little while after being dropped in?
st: Calcium reacts with water: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂.
Bubbles of hydrogen gas stick to the surface of the metal.
The bubbles make the calcium buoyant.
ex.a: Hydrogen bubbles stick to the calcium and make it float.

topics.rl: Copper and silver are used for jewellery and coins partly because they are low in the reactivity series and stay unreacted for a long time.

topics.t: Extraction of metals, corrosion and alloys
topics.h: Gold lies almost pure in the ground, but sodium hides inside salt — how reactive a metal is decides how we dig it out!
p: Minerals are natural compounds of metals; an ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably. Unwanted earthy impurities are called gangue.

Low reactivity metals (Hg, Cu) are obtained by heating their ores in air, e.g. cinnabar (HgS) gives mercury. Middle metals (Zn, Fe, Pb): sulphide ores are roasted (heated strongly in excess air) and carbonate ores calcined (heated in limited air) to get oxides, which are reduced with carbon.

The thermit reaction Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ releases so much heat that the iron forms molten, so it is used to join railway tracks. Highly reactive metals (Na, Mg, Ca, Al) are extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds.

Electrolytic refining: impure metal is the anode, a thin strip of pure metal is the cathode, and a salt solution of the metal is the electrolyte. Pure metal collects on the cathode; insoluble impurities settle as anode mud.

Corrosion: silver turns black (silver sulphide), copper turns green (basic copper carbonate) and iron rusts. It is prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising (zinc coating), chrome plating, anodising and making alloys such as stainless steel (iron + nickel + chromium), brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn) and solder (Pb + Sn).

ex.q: Think it through: why is a galvanised iron bucket protected from rusting even if its zinc coating gets scratched?
st: Galvanising coats iron with zinc.
Zinc is more reactive than iron.
Zinc corrodes in place of iron, so the exposed iron is still protected.
ex.a: Zinc, being more reactive, reacts first and continues to protect the iron.

topics.rl: The famous iron pillar near the Qutub Minar in Delhi has stood for centuries without rusting — a tribute to the skill of ancient Indian iron workers. Gold jewellery is usually 22 carat: 22 parts gold mixed with 2 parts copper or silver to make it harder.

topics.t: Covalent bonding and the versatile carbon
topics.h: Carbon is the ultimate team player — it shares instead of grabbing or giving away electrons!
p: Carbon (atomic number 6, configuration 2, 4) has 4 valence electrons. Gaining 4 (C⁴⁻) or losing 4 (C⁴⁺) needs too much energy, so carbon shares electrons.
A covalent bond forms when atoms share a pair of electrons. H₂ has a single bond, O₂ a double bond (2 shared pairs) and N₂ a triple bond (3 shared pairs).
Covalent compounds have weak forces between molecules, so they usually have low melting and boiling points and are poor conductors of electricity.
Tetravalency (valency 4) and catenation (bonding with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branches and rings) let carbon form a huge number of compounds. Its small size makes its bonds strong.

Allotropes of carbon: diamond (each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3-D network, hardest natural substance), graphite (each C bonded to 3 others in hexagonal layers, slippery and conducts electricity) and fullerenes like C₆₀, shaped like a football.

ex.q: Think it through: how many electrons are shared in a molecule of nitrogen, N₂?
st: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons (2, 5) and needs 3 more for an octet.
Each nitrogen atom contributes 3 electrons to sharing.
That makes 3 shared pairs — a triple bond.
3 pairs × 2 electrons = 6 electrons.
ex.a: 6 electrons (3 shared pairs, a triple bond)

topics.rl: The 'lead' in your pencil is actually graphite: its layers slide off onto paper. Diamonds cut glass and are used in drilling tools because they are so hard.

topics.t: Hydrocarbons, homologous series and functional groups
topics.h: Add one CH₂ at a time and you climb a ladder of compounds — methane, ethane, propane, butane!
p: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Saturated ones (alkanes, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) have only single bonds; unsaturated ones have a double bond (alkenes, CₙH₂ₙ) or a triple bond (alkynes, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).
Carbon chains can be straight, branched or ring-shaped (cyclohexane C₆H₁₂, benzene C₆H₆). Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are isomers — butane C₄H₁₀ has two.
A homologous series is a family with the same functional group in which each member differs from the next by –CH₂– (14 u). Chemical properties are similar; physical properties change gradually.
Functional groups give compounds their properties: halo (–Cl, –Br), alcohol (–OH), aldehyde (–CHO), ketone (>C=O) and carboxylic acid (–COOH).
Naming: the stem tells the number of carbons (meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4) and the ending or prefix tells the group: propanol, propanal, propanone, propanoic acid, chloropropane, propene.

ex.q: Think it through: name CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH.
st: Count carbons: 3, so the stem is 'propan-'.
The functional group is –OH, an alcohol, so the ending is '-ol'.
Put them together.
ex.a: Propanol

topics.rl: The LPG cylinder in your kitchen contains butane and propane, and CNG used in autos and buses is mainly methane — both members of the alkane family.

topics.t: Chemical properties, ethanol and ethanoic acid
topics.h: The same carbon compounds that burn in a gas stove can also turn into the sour vinegar in your pickle jar!
p: Combustion: carbon compounds burn in oxygen to give CO₂, water, heat and light. Saturated hydrocarbons generally burn with a clean flame; unsaturated ones give a yellow, sooty flame.
Oxidation: alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate (oxidising agents) convert ethanol into ethanoic acid.

Addition: unsaturated compounds add hydrogen in the presence of a nickel or palladium catalyst — this hydrogenation turns vegetable oils into solid fats. Substitution: in sunlight, chlorine replaces hydrogen in methane: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
Ethanol (C₂H₅OH): reacts with sodium to give sodium ethoxide and hydrogen; heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K it loses water to form ethene.

Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH): a weak acid; 5–8% solution in water is vinegar; pure acid can freeze in cold weather (glacial acetic acid). With ethanol and an acid catalyst it forms a sweet-smelling ester (esterification); esters with NaOH give back alcohol and a salt (saponification). It reacts with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give CO₂.

ex.q: Think it through: the bottom of Ma's cooking vessel is getting black. What is wrong with the burner?
st: Black soot appears when fuel burns incompletely.
Incomplete combustion happens when there is not enough air (oxygen).
So the air holes of the burner are probably blocked.
ex.a: The air holes are blocked, so the fuel is not getting enough oxygen; cleaning them gives a clean blue flame.

topics.rl: Pickles and chutneys use vinegar (dilute ethanoic acid) as a preservative, and many fruity smells in sweets and perfumes come from esters.

topics.h: Soap molecules are like tiny tadpoles: one end loves water, the other loves oil — together they kidnap the dirt!
p: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. They are made by saponification of fats or oils with sodium hydroxide.
A soap molecule has an ionic (hydrophilic) end that dissolves in water and a long hydrocarbon (hydrophobic) tail that dissolves in oil.
In water, soap molecules form clusters called micelles: tails point inward around the oily dirt, ionic ends face outward into the water, so the dirt is rinsed away.
Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with them to form an insoluble, sticky precipitate called scum, so more soap is wasted.

Detergents are generally sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions. Their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, so they work well even in hard water; they are used in shampoos and washing powders.

ex.q: Think it through: a student washes a muddy kurta with soap in tube-well water and sees a white curdy mass instead of lather. Why?
st: The tube-well water is probably hard, containing calcium and magnesium salts.
Soap reacts with these ions to form an insoluble precipitate (scum).
Soap is used up in forming scum, so little lather forms.
A detergent would work better here.
ex.a: The water is hard; soap forms scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions instead of lathering, so a detergent should be used.

topics.rl: When you wash greasy hands after eating samosas, soap micelles trap the oil inside them so water can carry it down the drain.

topics.h: A neem leaf is a solar-powered kitchen, and your gut is a 'food factory' with its own conveyor belt!
p: Autotrophs make their own food. In photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → (chlorophyll, sunlight) → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O. Extra carbohydrate is stored as starch.

Photosynthesis involves: light absorbed by chlorophyll; light energy changed to chemical energy and water split into hydrogen and oxygen; carbon dioxide reduced to carbohydrates. Gases pass through stomata, opened and closed by guard cells.

Heterotrophs depend on others: Amoeba engulfs food using pseudopodia into a food vacuole; fungi like bread mould break down food outside the body; parasites such as Cuscuta (amarbel), lice and tapeworms feed on a host.
Human digestion: saliva's salivary amylase breaks starch into sugar; the stomach's gastric glands release HCl (acidic medium), pepsin (digests proteins) and mucus (protects the lining).

In the small intestine, bile from the liver makes the food alkaline and emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice has trypsin (proteins) and lipase (fats); intestinal juice completes digestion to glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol. Villi absorb the food; the large intestine absorbs water.

ex.q: Think it through: a variegated (green-and-white) money-plant leaf is kept in sunlight, then tested with iodine. Which parts turn blue-black?
st: Iodine turns blue-black with starch.
Starch is made by photosynthesis, which needs chlorophyll.
Only the green parts have chlorophyll.
ex.a: Only the parts that were green turn blue-black, showing chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.

topics.rl: A cow chewing grass for hours has a much longer small intestine than a tiger, because the cellulose in grass takes longer to digest than meat.

topics.h: Every breath you take helps your cells 'burn' glucose without a single flame!
p: Respiration releases energy from food. First, glucose (6 carbons) is broken into pyruvate (3 carbons) in the cytoplasm.
Without oxygen: in yeast, pyruvate becomes ethanol + CO₂ (fermentation); in our muscles during hard exercise it becomes lactic acid, causing cramps.
With oxygen (aerobic), in the mitochondria, pyruvate is broken into CO₂ and water, releasing much more energy. Energy is stored as ATP, the energy currency of the cell.
Air path: nostrils (hairs and mucus filter dust) → throat → trachea (rings of cartilage stop it collapsing) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli, where gases are exchanged with blood.

Breathing in: ribs lift and the diaphragm flattens, making the chest cavity larger. Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen; CO₂ is more soluble in water and is carried mostly dissolved in blood. Aquatic animals breathe faster because water has less dissolved oxygen.

ex.q: Think it through: why do your legs ache with cramps after a fast 400 m race on Sports Day?
st: During a sprint muscles need energy faster than oxygen can reach them.
Muscle cells then break pyruvate without oxygen.
This produces lactic acid, which builds up and causes cramps.
ex.a: Lactic acid builds up from anaerobic respiration in muscles when oxygen runs short.

topics.rl: Idli and dosa batter rises overnight because yeast and bacteria respire anaerobically, releasing carbon dioxide that makes it fluffy.

topics.h: Your heart is a four-room pump that keeps beating your whole life without a single holiday!
p: Blood has plasma (carries food, CO₂ and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form), red blood cells (carry oxygen) and platelets (help blood clot to stop bleeding).

The human heart has four chambers. Right side: deoxygenated blood from the body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs. Left side: oxygenated blood from the lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → whole body. Valves stop backflow.

Blood passes through the heart twice per cycle (double circulation), keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate. Fish have a two-chambered heart; amphibians and many reptiles have three chambers.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick, elastic walls; veins bring blood back, have thinner walls and valves; capillaries are one cell thick. Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mm of Hg, measured with a sphygmomanometer. Lymph carries digested fat from the intestine and drains extra tissue fluid back into blood.

Plants: xylem carries water and minerals up from roots, pulled mainly by transpiration (evaporation of water from leaves) during the day; root pressure helps at night. Phloem carries food such as sucrose in both directions (translocation), using energy from ATP.

ex.q: Think it through: why do the ventricles have thicker muscular walls than the atria?
st: Atria only push blood a short distance, into the ventricles.
Ventricles pump blood out to the lungs and to the whole body.
That needs much more force, so they need thicker muscles.
ex.a: Ventricles must pump blood to distant organs, so they need thicker, stronger walls.

topics.rl: When a doctor wraps a cuff around your arm and pumps it up, she is measuring your blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer.

topics.h: Your two bean-shaped kidneys filter your blood all day — like a super-careful water purifier!
p: Excretion removes harmful nitrogenous wastes such as urea. The human excretory system: a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and the urethra.
Each kidney has many filtering units called nephrons. In each nephron, a cluster of capillaries (glomerulus) sits inside a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule, where blood is filtered.
As the filtrate passes along the tubule, useful substances like glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water are reabsorbed. The rest becomes urine, stored in the bladder.
If kidneys fail, an artificial kidney (haemodialysis) removes nitrogenous wastes from the blood by passing it through a dialysing fluid, but it does not reabsorb anything.
Plants excrete oxygen and water vapour through stomata, store wastes in vacuoles and in leaves that fall off, and store some wastes as resins and gums in old xylem.

ex.q: Think it through: about 180 litres of filtrate is formed in the kidneys every day, but only a litre or two of urine is passed. Where does the rest go?
st: The filtrate contains water, glucose, amino acids and salts along with urea.
Tubules of the nephron reabsorb useful substances and most of the water.
So only a small volume, rich in wastes, leaves as urine.
ex.a: Most of it is reabsorbed back into the blood by the kidney tubules.

topics.rl: The dark sticky resin oozing from a pine (chir) tree or the gum on a babool tree is partly how plants store their waste products.

topics.h: You pull your hand off a hot tawa before you even 'think' about it — your spinal cord took that decision!
p: Receptors in sense organs detect information — e.g. taste receptors (gustatory) on the tongue and smell receptors (olfactory) in the nose.

A neuron has dendrites (pick up information), a cell body, and a long axon. The message travels as an electrical impulse from dendrite → cell body → axon; at the axon end chemicals are released that cross the gap (synapse) to the next cell.

Reflex action: a quick, automatic response, e.g. withdrawing a hand from a flame. Path (reflex arc): receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in spinal cord → motor neuron → effector muscle. The message also reaches the brain.

Brain: the forebrain is the main thinking part, with areas for hearing, smell and sight and for controlling voluntary muscles. The hindbrain's medulla controls involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation and vomiting; the cerebellum keeps balance and posture and makes voluntary actions precise.

The brain is protected by the skull and a fluid-filled cushion; the spinal cord by the vertebral column. Muscles move because their cells contain special proteins that change shape and arrangement when a nerve impulse arrives.

ex.q: Think it through: you are riding a bicycle on a narrow lane and keep your balance. Which part of the brain is busiest?
st: Balance and posture are maintained by the cerebellum.
The cerebellum also makes voluntary movements precise, like steering.
So it is constantly adjusting your body on the cycle.
ex.a: The cerebellum, in the hindbrain

topics.rl: When the doctor taps just below your knee and your leg kicks up, she is testing a reflex arc that runs through your spinal cord.

topics.h: Your body has a postal service: tiny glands send chemical letters called hormones through your blood!
p: Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and released directly into the blood, so they reach cells all over the body.
Adrenaline (adrenal glands) prepares the body for an emergency: the heart beats faster, more blood goes to skeletal muscles and breathing becomes faster.
Thyroxine (thyroid) controls carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism. Making it needs iodine; lack of iodine can cause goitre (swollen neck), which is why we use iodised salt.

Growth hormone (pituitary) controls growth; its deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism. The hypothalamus releases a releasing factor that makes the pituitary secrete growth hormone. Testosterone (testes) and oestrogen (ovaries) bring about changes at puberty.

Insulin (pancreas) controls blood sugar; too little causes diabetes. Hormones work by feedback: when blood sugar rises, pancreatic cells detect it and release more insulin; when it falls, less is released.

ex.q: Think it through: a stray dog suddenly barks and chases you. Your heart pounds and you run faster than ever. Which hormone did this?
st: Emergencies trigger the adrenal glands.
They release adrenaline into the blood.
Adrenaline speeds up the heart and sends more blood and oxygen to muscles, preparing you to run.
ex.a: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands

topics.rl: The 'iodised' label on your salt packet is there because iodine helps the thyroid make thyroxine and prevents goitre.

topics.h: Plants have no nerves, yet a chhui-mui leaf folds when you touch it and sunflowers chase the light!
p: Plants respond without nerves. Touch-me-not (Mimosa pudica, chhui-mui) folds its leaves quickly by changing the amount of water in its cells — no growth is involved.

Tropisms are slow, growth-related movements towards or away from a stimulus: phototropism (light — shoots bend towards it), geotropism (gravity — roots grow down), hydrotropism (water) and chemotropism (chemicals, e.g. pollen tubes growing towards ovules).
Tendrils of a pea plant coil around a support because the part of the tendril away from the object grows faster than the part touching it.
Auxin is made at the shoot tip. When light comes from one side, auxin moves to the shady side, those cells grow longer, and the shoot bends towards light.
Gibberellins help stems grow; cytokinins promote cell division and are found in fruits and seeds; abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves.

ex.q: Think it through: a potted money plant on a window sill gradually bends towards the window. Explain.
st: Light falls on the shoot from one side.
Auxin collects on the shaded side of the shoot.
Cells on the shaded side grow longer than those on the lit side.
Unequal growth bends the shoot towards light — positive phototropism.
ex.a: Auxin makes cells on the shaded side grow longer, so the shoot bends towards the light.

topics.rl: Gardeners turn their pots every few days so plants on a balcony grow straight instead of leaning towards the light.

topics.h: A single Amoeba becomes two, a Bryophyllum leaf sprouts baby plants — some living things need no partner at all!
p: Reproduction makes copies of DNA, the blueprint of the body. Copying is never perfectly exact, so small variations arise; these help species survive when the environment changes.

Fission: in binary fission one cell splits into two (Amoeba can split in any plane; Leishmania, which causes kala-azar, splits in a definite plane). In multiple fission, as in Plasmodium (malaria parasite), one cell divides into many.
Fragmentation: a filament of Spirogyra breaks into pieces that grow into new individuals. Regeneration: Hydra and Planaria can regrow a whole body from a cut piece using specialised cells.

Budding: a bud grows out of the parent (Hydra, yeast) and later detaches. Spore formation: bread mould (Rhizopus) makes spores in sporangia; spores have thick walls that protect them until they reach moist surfaces.

Vegetative propagation: new plants from roots, stems or leaves — Bryophyllum buds in leaf notches; layering or grafting in sugarcane, roses and grapes. Such plants flower and fruit earlier and are genetically similar to the parent. Banana, orange, rose and jasmine are grown this way because they have lost the capacity to produce seeds.

ex.q: Think it through: why do gardeners grow jasmine (mogra) by layering or cuttings instead of from seed?
st: Jasmine has lost the capacity to produce seeds.
Vegetative propagation produces new plants from stems.
These plants flower earlier and are like the parent.
ex.a: Because jasmine cannot produce seeds, so it is propagated vegetatively — and it flowers sooner.

topics.rl: When stale bread grows a fuzzy black-grey layer, that is Rhizopus mould sending out countless spores — keep bread dry and covered!

topics.h: A hibiscus flower is a complete baby-making kit — and bees are the delivery partners!
p: Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents, giving more variation. Germ cells carry half the usual DNA, so the zygote gets the full amount.
Flower parts: stamens are male (anther makes pollen grains); the pistil (carpel) is female, with stigma, style and ovary containing ovules, each with an egg cell.
Bisexual flowers have both stamens and pistil (Hibiscus, mustard); unisexual flowers have only one (papaya, watermelon).

Pollination: transfer of pollen from anther to stigma — self-pollination (same flower) or cross-pollination (another flower) by wind, water or animals. A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule, and the male germ cell fuses with the egg (fertilisation) to form a zygote.

After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed (with an embryo) and the ovary ripens into the fruit; petals, sepals and stamens may wither and fall. In germination the radicle grows into the root and the plumule into the shoot, using food from the cotyledons.

ex.q: Think it through: a papaya tree in a garden never bears fruit, though it flowers every year. What could be the reason?
st: Papaya flowers are unisexual.
Some papaya plants bear only male flowers.
Without a pistil and ovary, no fruit can develop.
ex.a: It may be a male papaya plant whose flowers have only stamens, so no fruit forms.

topics.rl: Farmers keep beehives near mustard fields because bees carry pollen from flower to flower, improving cross-pollination.

topics.h: Growing up brings many changes — understanding them with science helps us stay healthy and respectful!
p: Puberty is the period when the reproductive organs mature and the body changes, e.g. growth of hair in new areas; in boys the voice deepens, and in girls breasts develop. It happens at different ages for different people.

Male system: testes make sperm and the hormone testosterone. They lie outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotum because sperm formation needs a lower temperature than normal body temperature. Sperm travel through the vas deferens; seminal vesicles and the prostate add fluid.

Female system: the two ovaries make oestrogen, and every month one of them releases an egg. The egg passes into the oviduct (fallopian tube), where fertilisation can occur. The embryo implants in the uterus and gets nutrition and oxygen from the mother through the placenta; development takes about nine months.
If the egg is not fertilised, the thickened, blood-rich lining of the uterus breaks down and comes out as menstruation, roughly every month, lasting about 2 to 8 days.

Reproductive health: some infections spread through sexual contact — bacterial (gonorrhoea, syphilis) and viral (warts, HIV-AIDS). Contraceptive methods include barriers such as condoms (which also reduce infection spread), hormonal pills, devices like the copper-T, and surgical methods (vasectomy, tubectomy). In India, the law bans finding out or revealing a baby's sex before birth, to prevent sex selection.

ex.q: Think it through: why are the testes located in the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity?
st: Sperm formation needs a temperature lower than normal body temperature.
The scrotum keeps the testes slightly outside the body.
So they stay cooler than the abdomen.
ex.a: Because sperm formation needs a lower temperature than the normal body temperature.

topics.rl: School health programmes and doctors encourage teenagers to ask questions about body changes openly — accurate information keeps everyone healthy.

topics.h: A monk with a garden of pea plants cracked the code of inheritance long before anyone had seen a gene!
p: Gregor Johann Mendel studied garden pea plants, choosing clear contrasting traits: tall/short plants, round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds, violet/white flowers.
He crossed a pure tall plant (TT) with a pure short plant (tt). All first-generation (F1) plants were tall (Tt) — none were medium height.
The trait that appears in F1 is dominant (tall, T); the hidden one is recessive (short, t). A recessive trait shows only when both copies are recessive (tt).
When F1 plants were self-pollinated, the F2 generation had tall and short plants in the ratio 3 : 1. Genotypes were TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1.
Conclusion: each trait is controlled by a pair of factors (now called genes), one from each parent; the short trait was not lost in F1, only hidden.

ex.q: Think it through: F1 tall plants (Tt) are self-pollinated and 400 F2 plants grow. About how many are short?
st: Cross Tt × Tt: offspring are TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
Only tt is short: 1 out of 4.
ex.a: About 100 short plants (and about 300 tall)

topics.rl: Farmers and scientists at Indian agricultural institutes use the same principles of inheritance to breed crops with useful traits like better yield.

topics.h: Your dimples, curly hair or ear shape are written in a coded instruction book you got from both parents!
p: A gene is a section of DNA that carries the instructions for a protein. Proteins control traits — e.g. a gene for an enzyme that makes a growth hormone affects plant height.
Each body cell has two copies of every gene, one from each parent. Both parents contribute almost equal amounts of genetic material to the child.
Genes lie on chromosomes. Germ cells get only one chromosome from each pair, so when two germ cells fuse, the full number is restored.
Dihybrid cross: round yellow (RRYY) × wrinkled green (rryy) → F1 all round yellow. In F2: round yellow 9, round green 3, wrinkled yellow 3, wrinkled green 1 — a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
New combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) show that traits are inherited independently. Sexual reproduction thus produces variations.

ex.q: Think it through: in a dihybrid F2 of 160 pea plants, about how many would have wrinkled green seeds?
st: The F2 ratio is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, a total of 16 parts.
Wrinkled green is 1 part.
ex.a: About 10 plants

topics.rl: Families often notice a grandparent's trait — like the same eye shape — skipping one generation and reappearing; recessive genes explain how that can happen.

topics.h: Whether a baby is a girl or a boy is decided at the very moment of fertilisation — by a tiny chromosome!
p: Different species decide sex in different ways. In some reptiles, the temperature at which fertilised eggs are kept decides the sex; some snails can change sex.
Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs are autosomes, and 1 pair is the sex chromosomes.
Females have a perfect pair of X chromosomes (XX). Males have one X and one shorter Y chromosome (XY).
Every egg from the mother carries an X. Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y.

If an X-sperm fertilises the egg, the child is a girl (XX); if a Y-sperm does, the child is a boy (XY). So the sex of the child is decided by which chromosome comes from the father, and the chance of each is 50%.

ex.q: Think it through: a family has three daughters. A relative says the mother is 'responsible'. What does science say?
st: The mother's eggs always carry an X chromosome.
Whether the child is a girl or a boy depends on whether the sperm carries X or Y.
Each birth is a separate 50 : 50 chance, so no one is to blame.
ex.a: Science shows the mother is not responsible: the child's sex depends on the chromosome in the sperm, and it is a matter of chance.

topics.rl: Knowing that sex is decided by chance and chromosomes helps us respect girls and boys equally — every child is welcome.

topics.h: A steel katori can be a funhouse mirror — look into the inside and outside of the bowl and your face changes!
p: Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane. These hold for all reflecting surfaces, including curved ones.
A plane mirror forms an image that is virtual, erect, the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.
A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere. Concave mirrors curve inward (reflecting surface caves in) and converge light; convex mirrors bulge outward and diverge light.

Key terms: pole (P) is the centre of the mirror's surface; centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the sphere; radius of curvature (R) is PC; the principal axis passes through P and C; the principal focus (F) is where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or seem to come from (convex).
For mirrors of small aperture, the radius of curvature is twice the focal length: R = 2f, so F lies midway between P and C.

ex.q: Think it through: a concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. Where is its principal focus?
st: Use R = 2f.
F lies on the principal axis midway between P and C.
ex.a: The focus is 15 cm from the pole, midway between P and C.

topics.rl: Torches and vehicle headlights use concave mirrors with the bulb at the focus so that a strong parallel beam is thrown forward.

topics.t: Images by spherical mirrors and the mirror formula
topics.h: Move closer to a concave shaving mirror and suddenly your face becomes giant — the position of the object decides everything!
p: Concave mirror images: object at infinity → image at F (point-sized, real, inverted); beyond C → between F and C (diminished); at C → at C (same size); between C and F → beyond C (enlarged); at F → at infinity; between P and F → behind the mirror, virtual, erect and enlarged.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image behind the mirror, between P and F.

New Cartesian sign convention: the pole is the origin; the object is placed to the left; distances measured in the direction of incident light (to the right) are positive, against it negative; heights above the axis are positive. So u is negative for real objects and f is negative for a concave mirror, positive for a convex mirror.
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification: m = h′/h = −v/u. Negative m means real and inverted; positive m means virtual and erect.
Uses: concave mirrors in torches, headlights, shaving mirrors, dentists' mirrors and solar furnaces; convex mirrors as rear-view mirrors because they give an erect image and a wider field of view.

ex.q: A 2 cm tall object is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.
st: Sign convention: u = −25 cm, f = −15 cm.
v = −37.5 cm: the image is 37.5 cm in front of the mirror.
Negative m: real and inverted; |m| > 1: enlarged.
ex.a: v = −37.5 cm; the image is real, inverted and enlarged (3 cm tall).

topics.rl: The curved mirrors at sharp turns on hill roads in Uttarakhand and Himachal are convex: they show a wide view of oncoming traffic.

topics.t: Refraction of light and refractive index
topics.h: A coin at the bottom of a bucket of water seems to float up — light is playing tricks as it changes speed!
p: Refraction is the change in direction of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another, because its speed changes. Light going along the normal does not bend.
Going from a rarer to a denser medium (air → glass), light slows down and bends towards the normal; from denser to rarer, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.
Laws of refraction: (1) the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; (2) Snell's law — sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media and a given colour of light.

Refractive index: n = speed of light in vacuum (c) ÷ speed of light in the medium (v). Relative refractive index n₂₁ = v₁/v₂. Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum. Some values: water 1.33, kerosene 1.44, crown glass 1.52, diamond 2.42.

Optical density is not mass density: kerosene floats on water yet is optically denser. In a rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways (lateral displacement).

ex.q: Think it through: the refractive index of a glass is 1.5. What is the speed of light in it?
st: n = c/v, so v = c/n.

topics.rl: A pencil dipped in a glass of water looks bent at the surface, and a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is — both are due to refraction.

topics.t: Lenses, the lens formula and power
topics.h: A magnifying glass can make an ant look like a dinosaur — and the same idea helps millions of people see clearly!
p: A convex lens is thicker at the middle and converges light; a concave lens is thinner at the middle and diverges light. Light through the optical centre (O) goes straight on.

Convex lens images: object at infinity → image at F₂ (point-sized); beyond 2F₁ → between F₂ and 2F₂ (diminished); at 2F₁ → at 2F₂ (same size); between F₁ and 2F₁ → beyond 2F₂ (enlarged); at F₁ → at infinity; between F₁ and O → same side as object, virtual, erect, enlarged (magnifying glass).
A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image between its focus and the optical centre, on the same side as the object.
Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Magnification: m = h′/h = v/u. Focal length is positive for a convex lens and negative for a concave lens.
Power P = 1/f, with f in metres; unit dioptre (D). A convex lens has positive power, a concave lens negative power. For lenses in contact, P = P₁ + P₂ + …

ex.q: An object is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image position and magnification.
st: v = +30 cm: real image on the other side of the lens.
m = v/u = 30 ÷ (−15) = −2: inverted and twice the size.
ex.a: v = +30 cm, m = −2: real, inverted and enlarged.

topics.rl: When an optometrist writes −1.5 on your prescription, it means a concave lens of power −1.5 D; a positive number would mean a convex lens.

topics.ch: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
topics.t: The human eye and defects of vision
topics.h: Your eye is a camera that refocuses itself in a split second — from your phone screen to a kite high in the sky!
p: Light enters through the cornea, where most of the refraction happens. The iris controls the size of the pupil, which regulates how much light enters. The eye lens fine-tunes the focus to form a real, inverted image on the retina; the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

Power of accommodation: ciliary muscles change the eye lens's focal length. Relaxed muscles make the lens thinner (longer focal length) for distant objects; contracted muscles make it thicker (shorter focal length) for near objects. For a young adult with normal vision, the near point is about 25 cm and the far point is at infinity.

Myopia (near-sightedness): distant objects look blurred because the image forms in front of the retina; caused by excessive curvature of the eye lens or elongation of the eyeball. Corrected with a concave lens.

Hypermetropia (far-sightedness): near objects look blurred because the image would form behind the retina; the near point is farther than 25 cm. Caused by too long a focal length of the eye lens or the eyeball being too small. Corrected with a convex lens.

Presbyopia: with age the ciliary muscles weaken and the lens becomes less flexible, so the near point recedes; corrected with convex lenses, or bifocals (concave upper part for distance, convex lower part for reading) if both defects exist. In cataract, the lens becomes milky and cloudy; surgery can restore vision.

ex.q: A student cannot see objects clearly beyond 2 m. What kind and power of lens does she need?
st: She has myopia: her far point is 2 m instead of infinity.
A concave lens must make distant objects appear to come from 2 m, so f = −2 m.
ex.a: A concave lens of power −0.5 D

topics.rl: Eye doctors advise taking breaks from screens and looking at distant objects now and then; if myopia does develop, spectacles with concave lenses correct it.

topics.ch: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
topics.t: Refraction through a prism and dispersion
topics.h: Shine sunlight through a glass prism and out pops a rainbow — white light was hiding seven colours all along!
p: A triangular glass prism has two inclined refracting faces; the angle between them is the angle of the prism. Light bends towards the base, and the angle between the incident and emergent rays is the angle of deviation.
Dispersion: white light splits into its component colours — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red (VIBGYOR). This band of colours is a spectrum.
Different colours bend by different amounts: red bends the least and violet the most.

Isaac Newton first used a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight. A second, identical prism placed upside down recombines the colours into white light, showing sunlight is made of seven colours.

A rainbow forms when tiny water droplets in the air after a shower act like small prisms: they refract and disperse sunlight, reflect it internally and refract it again. It is always seen opposite to the Sun.

ex.q: Think it through: you want to see a rainbow on a sunny morning while watering plants with a hose. Which way should you face?
st: A rainbow is formed by sunlight dispersed by water droplets.
The light is reflected back from inside the droplets towards the observer.
So the Sun must be behind you.
ex.a: Face away from the Sun (the Sun behind you), towards the water spray.

topics.rl: The glittering colours from the cut-glass pieces of a chandelier at a Diwali party are small displays of light splitting into colours, just like in a prism.

topics.ch: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
topics.h: Why is the sky blue and not green or red? Tiny air molecules are throwing blue light all around you!
p: Scattering: when light hits tiny particles, they send it off in different directions. The colour of scattered light depends on the size of the particles.
Tyndall effect: the path of a light beam becomes visible when it passes through a colloid, e.g. sunlight entering a smoky room or streaming through a dense forest canopy.

Very fine particles (such as air molecules) scatter mainly blue light, which has a shorter wavelength; larger particles scatter longer wavelengths; large enough particles make the scattered light look white.
The sky looks blue because air molecules and fine particles scatter blue light much more strongly than red light; red light's wavelength is about 1.8 times that of blue light.

Without an atmosphere there would be no scattering, so the sky would look dark — as astronauts at very high altitudes see. Red is used for danger signals because it is scattered the least by fog or smoke, so it can be seen from far away.

ex.q: Think it through: why are traffic stop lights and danger signals red?
st: Smoke and fog particles scatter light.
Red light has the longest wavelength among visible colours and is scattered least.
So red light travels farthest through fog and smoke and is seen from a distance.
ex.a: Red is scattered the least, so it stays visible from far away even in fog or smoke.

topics.rl: On a winter morning in Delhi, you can see bright beams of sunlight through the fog between trees — the Tyndall effect in action.

topics.t: Current, potential difference and Ohm's law
topics.h: Electricity in a wire is like water in a pipe: the 'push' is voltage, the flow is current, and narrow pipes resist!
p: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t. Its SI unit is the ampere (A); 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. Conventionally current flows from + to −, opposite to the flow of electrons. It is measured by an ammeter connected in series.
Potential difference (V) between two points is the work done to move a unit charge between them: V = W/Q. Its unit is the volt; 1 V = 1 J/C. It is measured by a voltmeter connected in parallel.

Ohm's law: at constant temperature, the current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it: V = IR. R is the resistance, measured in ohms (Ω); 1 Ω = 1 V/A.
Resistance of a uniform conductor: R = ρl/A. It increases with length (l), decreases with cross-sectional area (A) and depends on the material through its resistivity ρ (unit Ω m).

Metals like copper and aluminium have low resistivity and are used for wires; alloys like nichrome have higher resistivity and do not oxidise readily at high temperatures, so they are used in heating elements; glass and rubber are insulators.

ex.q: A bulb draws a current of 0.5 A from a 220 V supply. What is the resistance of its filament?
st: Ohm's law: R = V/I.

topics.rl: Electricians use copper wires inside your walls because copper has very low resistivity, so little energy is wasted as heat.

topics.h: Why can one fused bulb in a series string of fairy lights switch off the whole string, but your house lights stay on? Series vs parallel!
p: Series: resistors joined end to end. The same current flows through each; the total voltage is shared: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃. Equivalent resistance Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃, which is larger than any single resistor.
Parallel: resistors joined across the same two points. Each has the same potential difference; the total current divides: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃.
Equivalent resistance in parallel: 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃. Rₚ is smaller than the smallest individual resistance.
In series, if one component fails the whole circuit breaks, and all components share one current — unsuitable for appliances with different needs.
Homes use parallel wiring: each appliance gets the full mains voltage, draws its own current and can be switched on or off independently.

ex.q: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel to a 6 V battery. Find the equivalent resistance and the total current.
st: Rₚ = 2 Ω.
Check: 6 Ω carries 1 A and 3 Ω carries 2 A; 1 + 2 = 3 A.
ex.a: Rₚ = 2 Ω; total current = 3 A

topics.rl: If the fridge is switched off, the TV keeps working — because every socket in your home is connected in parallel.

topics.t: Heating effect of current and electric power
topics.h: Your geyser, iron and toaster all turn electricity into heat — and the electricity bill counts that energy in 'units'!
p: When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy turns into heat. Joule's law of heating: H = I²Rt. Heat produced is proportional to the square of current, to resistance and to time.

Uses: electric iron, toaster, oven, kettle and room heater. In a bulb, the tungsten filament (melting point 3380 °C) glows; bulbs are filled with chemically inactive nitrogen and argon to make the filament last longer.

A fuse is a safety device connected in series. Its wire is an alloy with a suitable melting point; when too much current flows, it melts and breaks the circuit. Home fuses are rated 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and so on.
Electric power is the rate of using electrical energy: P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Its unit is the watt (1 W = 1 V × 1 A = 1 J/s); 1 kW = 1000 W.
The commercial unit of energy is the kilowatt hour (kWh), the 'unit' on your bill: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

ex.q: An electric heater rated 1000 W is used for 2 hours a day. How many units of energy does it use in a day, and what is the cost at ₹6 per unit?
st: Power = 1000 W = 1 kW.
Energy = P × t = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh = 2 units.
ex.a: 2 units per day, costing ₹12

topics.rl: An electric iron rated 1000 W on a 220 V line draws about 4.5 A, so it needs a fuse rated 5 A — this is why fuse ratings matter.

topics.h: In 1820 a compass needle twitched near a wire carrying current — and electricity and magnetism turned out to be best friends!
p: A compass needle is a small bar magnet; its north-seeking end is its north pole. The space around a magnet where its force can be detected is its magnetic field — it has both strength and direction.

Magnetic field lines come out of the north pole and go into the south pole outside the magnet, and run from south to north inside it, so they are closed curves. Where lines are crowded the field is stronger. Two field lines never cross, because a compass cannot point in two directions at one place.
Hans Christian Oersted found in 1820 that a compass needle deflects near a wire carrying current — a current produces a magnetic field.

Around a straight current-carrying wire, field lines are concentric circles. Right-hand thumb rule: hold the wire in your right hand with the thumb along the current; your curled fingers show the direction of the field. The field is stronger for a larger current and weaker farther from the wire.

For a circular loop, the circles near the wire grow larger towards the centre, where the lines look nearly straight. The field of a coil increases with the number of turns, since the fields of the turns add up.

ex.q: Think it through: current flows vertically upward in a straight wire passing through a horizontal card. Which way do the field lines circle when seen from above?
st: Point your right thumb upward along the current.
Your fingers curl around the wire.
Seen from above, the curl is anticlockwise.
ex.a: Anticlockwise when viewed from above.

topics.rl: When you sprinkle iron filings on paper over a bar magnet in the school lab, they line up along the field lines, making the invisible field visible.

topics.t: Solenoid, electromagnet and force on a conductor
topics.h: Wrap wire around an iron nail, connect a cell, and pick up pins — you just built a magnet you can switch off!
p: A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound closely in the shape of a cylinder. Its field pattern is like a bar magnet's: one end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
Inside a solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, so the field is uniform there.
An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft iron core. It is a strong magnet only while current flows, and its strength can be increased with more current or more turns.
A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. The force is greatest when the current is perpendicular to the field, and reversing the current or the field reverses the force.

Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular. Forefinger → field, middle finger → current, thumb → direction of motion (force). Loudspeakers and measuring instruments use this force.

ex.q: Think it through: a wire carries current from left to right across a magnetic field pointing into the page. Which way is the force?
st: Use Fleming's left-hand rule.
Forefinger: into the page (field).
Middle finger: left to right (current).
Thumb then points upward, towards the top of the page.
ex.a: The force is upward (towards the top of the page).

topics.rl: Cranes in scrap yards use huge electromagnets to lift heavy iron pieces, then simply switch off the current to drop them.

topics.h: Behind every switchboard at home is a careful plan of three colour-coded wires that keep you safe!
p: Direct current (DC), from cells, flows in one direction. Alternating current (AC) reverses direction periodically. In India, AC has a frequency of 50 Hz — it changes direction every 1/100 second.
An advantage of AC over DC: electric power can be transmitted over long distances without much loss of energy.

Mains supply comes through a live wire (red insulation) and a neutral wire (black insulation); the potential difference between them in India is 220 V. The earth wire (green insulation) connects to a metal plate deep in the earth.

The earth wire is attached to metal bodies of appliances like irons, toasters and refrigerators. If the live wire touches the body, current flows safely to earth through this low-resistance path, so the user does not get a severe shock.

Homes have a 15 A circuit for high-power appliances (geysers, air coolers) and a 5 A circuit for bulbs and fans. Appliances are connected in parallel, each with its own switch. A fuse protects against short-circuiting (live and neutral wires touching) and overloading (too many appliances on one socket, or a sudden rise in supply voltage).

ex.q: Think it through: why is an electric iron with a metal body connected with a three-pin plug?
st: The third pin connects the metal body to the earth wire.
If current leaks to the metal body, the earth wire gives it a low-resistance path to the ground.
So the body stays at the earth's potential and the user is protected from a severe shock.
ex.a: The third (earth) pin safely carries any leaking current to the ground.

topics.rl: Never plug a heater, an iron and a kettle into one extension board together — that can overload the circuit and is a common cause of electrical fires.

topics.t: Ecosystems, food chains and energy flow
topics.h: In the Sundarbans, a tiger's dinner depends on deer, which depend on grass, which depends on the Sun — everything is connected!
p: An ecosystem is made of all living things (biotic components) in an area together with non-living (abiotic) factors such as temperature, rainfall, wind and soil. Forests, ponds and lakes are natural ecosystems; gardens, crop fields and aquariums are artificial ones.

Producers (green plants and blue-green algae) make food by photosynthesis. Consumers eat others: herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and parasites. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead remains and return nutrients to the soil.

A food chain shows who eats whom, e.g. grass → deer → lion. Each step is a trophic level: producers (1st), herbivores or primary consumers (2nd), small carnivores or secondary consumers (3rd), large carnivores or tertiary consumers (4th). Food chains interlink to form food webs.

Green plants capture only about 1% of the sunlight falling on their leaves. The 10 percent law: only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next; the rest is used for life processes or lost as heat.
So energy flow is unidirectional (it never returns to the Sun or to the plants), food chains usually have only three or four steps, and there are fewer organisms at higher trophic levels.

ex.q: In a food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the grass traps 10,000 J of energy. How much energy reaches the snake?
st: By the 10 percent law, each level passes on about 10%.
Grasshopper: 10% of 10,000 J = 1000 J.
Snake: 10% of 100 J = 10 J.
ex.a: About 10 J

topics.rl: In a farm pond in a village, algae feed tiny animals, which feed small fish, which feed larger fish and kingfishers — a complete aquatic food chain.

topics.h: High above us, a thin blanket of a special form of oxygen acts like sunscreen for the whole planet!
p: Ozone (O₃) is a molecule of three oxygen atoms. At higher levels of the atmosphere it shields the Earth from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation of the Sun, which can cause skin cancer in humans.
Ozone forms when UV radiation splits oxygen molecules: O₂ → O + O; then a free oxygen atom joins an oxygen molecule: O + O₂ → O₃.
Ozone is useful high in the atmosphere, but at ground level it is a deadly poison.
The amount of ozone began to drop sharply in the 1980s. This was linked to synthetic chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers.
In 1987, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) got countries to agree to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels. Today, CFC-free refrigerators are mandatory throughout the world.

ex.q: Think it through: why should old refrigerators and ACs be handed over to proper recyclers rather than broken open in a scrapyard?
st: Older refrigerators and ACs may contain CFC refrigerants.
If released, CFCs rise and damage the ozone layer.
A thinner ozone layer lets more harmful UV radiation reach the Earth.
ex.a: To stop any CFCs inside from escaping and damaging the ozone layer.

topics.rl: India is one of the many countries that has phased out the production of CFCs under international agreements, so new fridges and ACs sold today are CFC-free.

topics.h: Peels in a compost pit become rich soil, but a plastic bag thrown today may still be around when you are a grandparent!
p: Biodegradable substances (vegetable peels, leaves, paper, cotton) are broken down by biological processes such as the action of bacteria and fungi.
Non-biodegradable substances (most plastics, glass, some pesticides) are not broken down by these processes. They persist for a long time and can harm living things in the ecosystem.

Biological magnification: non-biodegradable chemicals like some pesticides enter the food chain and are not broken down or excreted, so they build up at each trophic level. Humans, at the top of many food chains, can end up with the highest concentration.

Managing waste: segregate wet (biodegradable) and dry waste at home, compost kitchen waste, reduce single-use plastic, reuse items like glass jars and cloth bags, and send paper, plastic and metal for recycling.
Even 'natural' choices need thought: replacing materials on a very large scale can create new problems, so the best solution is often to reduce waste in the first place.

ex.q: Think it through: a pesticide sprayed on crops is found at a higher concentration in fish-eating birds than in the water of the nearby lake. Why?
st: The pesticide is non-biodegradable, so it is not broken down.
Small organisms absorb it; fish eat many of them; birds eat many fish.
At each level the chemical is stored and accumulates, increasing in concentration.
ex.a: Biological magnification: the chemical builds up at each higher trophic level.

topics.rl: Many Indian cities ask households to keep separate bins for wet and dry waste so that kitchen waste can be composted and dry waste recycled.

qa.q: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
qa.a: Because mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction
qa.e: The law of conservation of mass says total mass stays the same, so every atom present before the reaction must still be there after it.

qa.q: Which of these is a correctly balanced equation?
qa.e: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O on each side.

qa.q: In 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂, how many hydrogen atoms are on the left side?
qa.e: The coefficient 4 multiplies everything in H₂O, and each H₂O has 2 H atoms: 4 × 2 = 8.

qa.q: While balancing, a student changes H₂O to H₂O₂ to get more oxygen. What is wrong?
qa.a: It changes the substance itself; only coefficients may be changed
qa.e: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. Balancing is done by putting numbers in front of formulae, never by altering subscripts.

qa.q: What does the symbol (aq) mean in NaCl(aq)?
qa.e: (aq) stands for aqueous, meaning the substance is dissolved in water.

qa.q: Which observation does NOT by itself show that a chemical reaction has happened?
qa.a: Ice melting into water in a glass
qa.e: Melting ice is only a change of state of the same substance (water); no new substance forms.

qa.q: In 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂, how many oxygen atoms are there on the right side?
qa.e: 2PbO gives 2, 4NO₂ gives 8 and O₂ gives 2, so 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 — the same as 2 × 6 = 12 on the left.

qa.q: Which balanced equation correctly shows aluminium burning in oxygen?
qa.e: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ has 4 Al and 6 O on each side.

qa.q: Quicklime reacts vigorously with water, releasing a lot of heat. Which type of reaction is this?
qa.e: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ joins two reactants into one product and gives out heat.

qa.q: Heating lead nitrate gives off brown fumes. What are these fumes?
qa.e: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is the brown gas; oxygen is colourless.

qa.q: White silver chloride turns grey in sunlight. What type of reaction is this?
qa.e: Light splits silver chloride into silver and chlorine: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂. This idea was used in black-and-white photography.

qa.q: Which is a double displacement reaction?
qa.e: Here the two compounds swap ions: sodium joins chloride and barium joins sulphate. BaSO₄ forms a white precipitate.

qa.q: Why does a white solid form when sodium sulphate and barium chloride solutions are mixed?
qa.a: Barium sulphate formed is insoluble in water
qa.e: A precipitate is an insoluble product. Barium sulphate does not dissolve, so it appears as a white solid; sodium chloride stays dissolved.

qa.q: Which of these is an endothermic process?
qa.a: Decomposition of calcium carbonate into lime
qa.e: Calcium carbonate must be heated strongly to break into CaO and CO₂, so it absorbs heat.

qa.q: Zinc granules are added to dilute sulphuric acid. Which gas is released?
qa.e: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Zinc displaces hydrogen from the acid.

qa.q: In the electrolysis of water, which gas collects at the electrode where the volume is larger?
qa.e: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, so hydrogen's volume is twice that of oxygen.

qa.q: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, which substance is oxidised?
qa.e: Hydrogen gains oxygen to become water, so hydrogen is oxidised. Copper oxide loses oxygen and is reduced.

qa.q: Brown copper powder is heated in a china dish in air. What does it turn into?
qa.e: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. Copper gains oxygen and the surface becomes black copper(II) oxide.

qa.q: In MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + 2H₂O + Cl₂, what happens to HCl?
qa.a: It is oxidised because it loses hydrogen
qa.e: HCl loses hydrogen to become Cl₂; loss of hydrogen is oxidation. MnO₂ loses oxygen, so it is reduced.

qa.q: Which two things are needed for iron to rust?
qa.e: Iron rusts only when both air (oxygen) and moisture are present. Without either one, rusting stops.

qa.q: Why do chips makers fill packets with nitrogen?
qa.a: To keep oxygen away so the oil does not turn rancid
qa.e: Nitrogen is unreactive. Replacing air with it keeps oxygen away, slowing oxidation of fats and oils.

qa.q: A copper vessel left in moist air for months gets a green coating. This is an example of —
qa.e: Copper reacts slowly with moist carbon dioxide in air, forming a green basic copper carbonate layer — corrosion.

qa.q: In ZnO + C → Zn + CO, the substance reduced is —
qa.e: Zinc oxide loses oxygen to form zinc, so ZnO is reduced.

qa.q: Which statement about a redox reaction is correct?
qa.a: Oxidation and reduction take place together
qa.e: If one substance gains oxygen, another must lose it in the same reaction, so oxidation and reduction occur together.

qa.q: What is the pH of pure water?
qa.e: Pure water is neutral; neutral solutions have pH 7.

qa.q: A few drops of phenolphthalein are added to a solution and it turns pink. The solution is —
qa.e: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acids and neutral solutions and turns pink in bases.

qa.q: Which of these is an olfactory indicator?
qa.e: Olfactory indicators change smell. Vanilla's smell cannot be detected in a basic solution.

qa.q: Rain is called acid rain when its pH is less than —
qa.e: Rain with a pH below 5.6 is called acid rain; when it flows into rivers it can make survival of aquatic life difficult.

qa.q: A honeybee sting injects an acid. What is a sensible remedy?
qa.a: Rubbing a mild base like baking soda solution
qa.e: The sting contains methanoic acid; a mild base such as baking soda neutralises it.

qa.q: Dry HCl gas does not change the colour of dry blue litmus paper. Why?
qa.a: Without water, HCl does not produce H⁺ ions
qa.e: Acidic behaviour appears only when H⁺ ions form, and that needs water.

qa.q: Why should acid be added slowly to water, and not water to acid, when diluting?
qa.a: Because the process gives out a lot of heat and adding water to acid can make it splash
qa.e: Dilution of a concentrated acid is highly exothermic. Adding water to acid can boil the water locally and spray acid out.

qa.q: Solution P has pH 9 and solution Q has pH 12. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Q is more basic than P
qa.e: Above 7 is basic, and the higher the pH, the more basic the solution, so Q (pH 12) is more basic.

qa.q: What are the products when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
qa.e: This is neutralisation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

qa.q: Dilute HCl is poured on marble chips (calcium carbonate). The gas given off —
qa.e: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O. Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky.

qa.q: Zinc granules heated with sodium hydroxide solution give —
qa.e: 2NaOH + Zn → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂. Zinc reacts with the base to release hydrogen.

qa.q: Copper oxide (black) is added to dilute HCl and stirred. The solution turns blue-green. What forms?
qa.e: CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O. A metal oxide reacts with an acid like a base, giving salt and water.

qa.q: Which salt gives a basic solution in water?
qa.e: Sodium carbonate comes from a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (carbonic acid), so its solution is basic.

qa.q: How many molecules of water of crystallisation are present in one formula unit of blue copper sulphate?
qa.e: Blue copper sulphate crystals are CuSO₄·5H₂O.

qa.q: Why do acidic solutions conduct electricity?
qa.a: They contain ions such as H⁺
qa.e: In water, acids produce ions, and moving ions carry the current.

qa.q: Which pair are both members of the 'sodium family' of salts?
qa.e: Salts with the same positive radical belong to one family; both contain sodium.

qa.q: Which gas is produced at the cathode in the chlor-alkali process?
qa.e: Hydrogen gas forms at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, and sodium hydroxide solution near the cathode.

qa.q: Why does a cake become soft and spongy when baking powder is used?
qa.a: Carbon dioxide released on heating makes it rise
qa.e: Heat and moisture make baking soda release CO₂; the gas bubbles puff up the batter. Tartaric acid neutralises the bitter sodium carbonate.

qa.q: What is the chemical formula of washing soda?
qa.e: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, with 10 water molecules.

qa.q: Which is a use of bleaching powder?
qa.e: Bleaching powder releases chlorine and kills germs, so it is used to disinfect water. It also bleaches cotton and linen.

qa.q: What happens when Plaster of Paris is mixed with water?
qa.a: It forms gypsum and sets into a hard mass
qa.e: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O, a hard solid.

qa.q: On heating, baking soda gives sodium carbonate, water and —
qa.e: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.

qa.q: The name 'chlor-alkali' comes from the products —
qa.e: Chlor stands for chlorine and alkali for sodium hydroxide, two of the products.

qa.q: Which salt is used in soda-acid fire extinguishers and as an antacid?
qa.e: Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) is a mild base and releases CO₂ with acids.

qa.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
qa.e: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Gallium melts only when warmed, as on a palm.

qa.q: Which non-metal is a good conductor of electricity?
qa.e: Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity — an exception among non-metals.

qa.q: Which oxide is amphoteric?
qa.e: Zinc oxide (like aluminium oxide) reacts with both acids and bases to form salt and water.

qa.q: Why are electric cooking pans often given handles of plastic or wood?
qa.a: Plastic and wood are poor conductors of heat, so the handle stays cool
qa.e: The metal body conducts heat to the food, while the poorly conducting handle protects your hand.

qa.q: The property that allows metals to be drawn into thin wires is called —
qa.e: Ductility is being drawn into wires; malleability is being beaten into sheets.

qa.q: A metal that can be cut with a knife is —
qa.e: Sodium and potassium are soft metals that can be cut with a knife.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a property of most non-metals?
qa.e: Sonority (ringing sound when struck) is a property of metals, which is why temple bells are made of metal.

qa.q: Which is the hardest natural substance known?
qa.e: Diamond, a form of carbon (a non-metal), is the hardest natural substance and has a very high melting point.

qa.q: Which metal reacts violently with cold water?
qa.e: Potassium is at the top of the series and reacts so vigorously with cold water that the hydrogen catches fire.

qa.q: An iron nail is dipped in zinc sulphate solution. What happens?
qa.a: No reaction, because zinc is more reactive than iron
qa.e: Only a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive one. Zinc is above iron, so iron cannot push it out.

qa.q: What is the ratio of concentrated HCl to concentrated HNO₃ in aqua regia?
qa.e: Aqua regia is freshly mixed 3 parts concentrated hydrochloric acid to 1 part concentrated nitric acid.

qa.q: Why is hydrogen usually NOT evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid?
qa.a: Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent and oxidises the hydrogen to water
qa.e: HNO₃ oxidises the hydrogen formed into water and itself is reduced to nitrogen oxides.

qa.q: What is the electronic configuration of the sodium ion, Na⁺?
qa.e: Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses its single outer electron to form Na⁺ with a stable 2, 8 arrangement.

qa.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but its solution in water does. Why?
qa.a: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions; in solution they can move
qa.e: Ions are present in the solid but locked in place by strong attraction. Dissolving lets them move and carry charge.

qa.q: Which metal reacts with steam but NOT with cold or hot water?
qa.e: Iron reacts with steam: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. Silver does not react even with steam.

qa.q: Ionic compounds generally dissolve in —
qa.e: Ionic compounds are soluble in water but generally insoluble in kerosene and petrol.

qa.q: What is gangue?
qa.a: Earthy impurities such as soil and sand in an ore
qa.e: Ores dug from the earth carry unwanted rock, soil and sand, called gangue, which must be removed first.

qa.q: Heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air is called —
qa.e: Calcination converts carbonate ores to oxides, e.g. ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂. Roasting is for sulphide ores in excess air.

qa.q: Why can't sodium be obtained by heating its oxide with carbon?
qa.a: Sodium has more attraction for oxygen than carbon has
qa.e: Sodium is very high in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot remove oxygen from it. Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride is used.

qa.q: In electrolytic refining of copper, the cathode is —
qa.a: A thin strip of pure copper
qa.e: Pure copper from the solution deposits on the thin pure copper cathode; the impure copper is the anode.

qa.q: Which reaction is used to join broken railway tracks?
qa.e: The thermit reaction gives so much heat that iron forms in the molten state and fills the gap.

qa.q: Silver ornaments turn black over time because they react with —
qa.e: Silver reacts with sulphur compounds in air to form a black coating of silver sulphide.

qa.q: Galvanisation means coating iron or steel with —
qa.e: A thin zinc layer protects iron from rusting even if scratched.

qa.q: Why is solder used to join electrical wires?
qa.a: It has a low melting point
