qa.e: Solder (lead + tin) melts at a low temperature, so it can be melted easily to join wires. Alloys often melt at lower temperatures than their pure metals.

qa.q: Why does carbon form covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds?
qa.a: Gaining or losing 4 electrons needs too much energy, so it shares them
qa.e: With 4 valence electrons, forming C⁴⁻ or C⁴⁺ is very difficult, so carbon reaches a stable octet by sharing.

qa.q: How many covalent bonds does one carbon atom form in methane (CH₄)?
qa.e: Carbon is tetravalent: it shares one electron pair with each of the 4 hydrogen atoms.

qa.q: Which molecule contains a double bond?
qa.e: Each oxygen (2, 6) needs 2 electrons, so two pairs are shared — a double bond. N₂ has a triple bond.

qa.q: Covalent compounds generally have —
qa.a: Low melting points and are poor conductors of electricity
qa.e: Forces between covalent molecules are weak, and no ions are formed, so melting points are low and electricity is not conducted.

qa.q: The property of carbon atoms to link with other carbon atoms to form long chains is called —
qa.e: Catenation is self-linking to form chains, branches and rings. Tetravalency means valency 4.

qa.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
qa.a: Graphite has free electrons because each carbon bonds to only three others
qa.e: In graphite each carbon uses three electrons for bonding with neighbours, leaving electrons free to move. In diamond all four are used.

qa.q: C₆₀, shaped like a football, belongs to which group of carbon allotropes?
qa.e: C₆₀ is a fullerene, named after the architect Buckminster Fuller whose domes it resembles.

qa.q: How many shared pairs of electrons are there in a molecule of N₂?
qa.e: Nitrogen (2, 5) needs 3 electrons, so the two atoms share 3 pairs — a triple bond.

qa.q: What is the molecular formula of propane?
qa.e: Propane is an alkane with 3 carbons: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ gives C₃H₈.

qa.q: Which of these is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
qa.e: Ethene (C₂H₄) has a carbon–carbon double bond, so it is unsaturated.

qa.q: By how many mass units (u) do two successive members of a homologous series differ?
qa.e: They differ by –CH₂–: 12 + 2 × 1 = 14 u.

qa.q: Butane and isobutane both have the formula C₄H₁₀ but different structures. They are called —
qa.e: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements.

qa.q: What is the correct name of CH₃COCH₃?
qa.e: It has 3 carbons with a ketone group in the middle, so it is propanone (commonly acetone).

qa.q: Which functional group is present in ethanoic acid?
qa.e: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) has the carboxylic acid group, –COOH.

qa.q: What is the general formula of alkynes?
qa.e: Alkynes have one triple bond and follow CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, e.g. ethyne C₂H₂.

qa.q: Which statement about a homologous series is correct?
qa.a: Members show similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties
qa.e: Same functional group gives similar chemistry; growing chain length makes melting and boiling points rise gradually.

qa.q: Which hydrocarbon is most likely to burn with a yellow, sooty flame?
qa.e: Ethyne is unsaturated (triple bond); unsaturated hydrocarbons give a yellow flame with lots of black smoke.

qa.q: Alkaline potassium permanganate converts ethanol into —
qa.e: KMnO₄ is an oxidising agent; it oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid.

qa.q: Hydrogenation of vegetable oil is an example of —
qa.e: Hydrogen adds across the double bonds of unsaturated oils, using a nickel catalyst.

qa.q: What forms when ethanol is heated at 443 K with excess concentrated sulphuric acid?
qa.e: Concentrated sulphuric acid removes water from ethanol (dehydration), giving ethene.

qa.q: Why is pure ethanoic acid called glacial acetic acid?
qa.a: It freezes into ice-like crystals in cold weather
qa.e: Its melting point is 290 K (about 17 °C), so it often freezes in winter, looking like a glacier.

qa.q: Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst. The product is —
qa.e: This is esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ester ethyl ethanoate smells sweet.

qa.q: In sunlight, methane and chlorine react to form chloromethane and HCl. This is a —
qa.e: A chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom, so it is substitution.

qa.q: What gas is evolved when ethanoic acid is added to sodium carbonate?
qa.e: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. CO₂ turns lime water milky.

qa.q: Soaps are —
qa.a: Sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids
qa.e: Soap is made by saponifying fats or oils with alkali, giving salts of long-chain fatty acids.

qa.q: In a micelle, the hydrocarbon tails of soap molecules point —
qa.e: The hydrophobic tails avoid water and cluster around the oil at the centre, while the ionic heads face the water.

qa.q: Why does soap not lather well in hard water?
qa.a: Soap reacts with calcium and magnesium salts to form scum
qa.e: The insoluble precipitate (scum) uses up soap, so little lather forms.

qa.q: Which part of a soap molecule is hydrophilic (water-loving)?
qa.e: The ionic (charged) end interacts with water; the hydrocarbon chain is hydrophobic.

qa.q: Why are detergents preferred for washing clothes in hard water?
qa.a: Their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions
qa.e: Detergents stay effective because they do not form scum with hardness ions.

qa.q: The reaction of an oil or fat with sodium hydroxide to make soap is called —
qa.e: Saponification means 'soap-making': esters of fatty acids react with alkali to give soap and glycerol.

qa.q: A sample of water gives a lot of curdy white precipitate and little lather with soap. The water is —
qa.e: Curdy precipitate (scum) is a sign of calcium and magnesium salts — hard water.

qa.q: Why can't plain water alone wash oily dirt off a plate?
qa.a: Oil does not dissolve in water, and without soap no micelles form to carry it
qa.e: Oil and water do not mix. Soap is needed to form micelles that hold oil in water as an emulsion.

qa.q: Which raw materials are needed for photosynthesis?
qa.e: Plants use carbon dioxide and water, with sunlight and chlorophyll, to make glucose and release oxygen.

qa.q: What opens and closes the stomata?
qa.e: Guard cells swell when water flows into them (pore opens) and shrink when they lose water (pore closes).

qa.q: Desert plants keep stomata closed during the day. How do they get CO₂ for photosynthesis?
qa.a: They take in CO₂ at night and store it as an intermediate for daytime use
qa.e: Opening stomata at night reduces water loss; the stored CO₂ is used when sunlight is available.

qa.q: Which enzyme in saliva begins the digestion of starch?
qa.e: Salivary amylase breaks down starch into sugar in the mouth.

qa.q: What is the role of mucus in the stomach?
qa.a: Protects the inner lining from acid
qa.e: Mucus protects the stomach lining from being damaged by hydrochloric acid.

qa.q: Bile juice does NOT contain enzymes, yet it helps digestion. How?
qa.a: It emulsifies large fat globules into smaller ones and makes the medium alkaline
qa.e: Bile salts break fats into small droplets so lipase can act, and bile neutralises the acidic food from the stomach.

qa.q: Why is the inner lining of the small intestine covered with villi?
qa.a: To increase the surface area for absorption
qa.e: Finger-like villi greatly increase the absorbing surface and are richly supplied with blood vessels.

qa.q: Cuscuta (amarbel) growing on other plants is an example of —
qa.e: Cuscuta draws its food from the host plant it grows on, so it is a parasite.

qa.q: Where does the first step of breaking glucose into pyruvate take place?
qa.e: Glucose is split into pyruvate in the cytoplasm; further aerobic breakdown happens in the mitochondria.

qa.q: How many carbon atoms does a pyruvate molecule have?
qa.e: One 6-carbon glucose splits into two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules.

qa.q: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
qa.e: Yeast ferments pyruvate into ethanol and CO₂ without oxygen.

qa.q: Why do the walls of the trachea have rings of cartilage?
qa.a: To make sure the air passage does not collapse
qa.e: Cartilage rings keep the trachea open so air can always flow.

qa.q: Which molecule is called the energy currency of the cell?
qa.e: Energy released in respiration is stored in ATP and used for cell activities.

qa.q: Why do fish breathe much faster than land animals?
qa.a: The amount of oxygen dissolved in water is much lower than in air
qa.e: Dissolved oxygen in water is low, so aquatic animals must move water over gills quickly.

qa.q: What happens during inhalation (breathing in)?
qa.a: Ribs lift and the diaphragm flattens, enlarging the chest cavity
qa.e: A bigger chest cavity lowers the pressure inside, so air rushes into the lungs.

qa.q: Which pigment carries oxygen in human blood?
qa.e: Haemoglobin in red blood cells has a very high affinity for oxygen.

qa.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
qa.e: The human heart has two atria and two ventricles — four chambers.

qa.q: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body?
qa.e: The left ventricle receives oxygen-rich blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the aorta.

qa.q: Why is separating oxygenated and deoxygenated blood useful for birds and mammals?
qa.a: It gives a highly efficient oxygen supply needed to keep a constant body temperature
qa.e: Birds and mammals use a lot of energy to maintain body temperature, so they need efficient oxygen delivery.

qa.q: What is the main force that pulls water up through the xylem of a tall tree during the day?
qa.e: Evaporation of water from leaves creates a suction that pulls water up the xylem.

qa.q: Which blood vessels have valves to prevent the backflow of blood?
qa.e: Blood in veins is under low pressure, so valves keep it flowing towards the heart.

qa.q: What does lymph do?
qa.a: Carries digested and absorbed fat and drains extra tissue fluid back into blood
qa.e: Lymph collects fluid that leaks out of capillaries and carries absorbed fat from the intestine.

qa.q: Translocation in plants refers to —
qa.e: Translocation is the movement of soluble products of photosynthesis through phloem, using energy from ATP.

qa.q: Which part of blood helps stop bleeding from a cut?
qa.e: Platelets help blood to clot at the site of injury.

qa.q: What is the basic filtering unit of the kidney?
qa.e: Each kidney contains a large number of nephrons that filter the blood.

qa.q: What is reabsorbed from the filtrate as it moves along the tubule?
qa.a: Glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water
qa.e: Useful substances return to the blood; wastes stay behind to form urine.

qa.q: Which is the correct path of urine?
qa.e: Urine forms in the kidney, travels down the ureter, is stored in the bladder and leaves through the urethra.

qa.q: How does haemodialysis differ from a real kidney?
qa.a: It filters blood but does not reabsorb useful substances
qa.e: The artificial kidney only removes wastes through a dialysing fluid; there is no reabsorption.

qa.q: Where does blood get filtered in a nephron?
qa.a: In the glomerulus inside Bowman's capsule
qa.e: The glomerulus is a ball of capillaries; filtration happens into the surrounding Bowman's capsule.

qa.q: Which is NOT a way plants get rid of wastes?
qa.e: Plants have no excretory organs like a bladder; they use leaves, vacuoles, gums, resins and stomata.

qa.q: The main nitrogenous waste removed by human kidneys is —
qa.e: Urea, a nitrogen-containing waste, is removed in urine.

qa.q: The amount of water reabsorbed in the kidneys depends on —
qa.a: How much excess water the body has and how much waste needs to be dissolved
qa.e: The body adjusts reabsorption to keep its water balance, so urine volume changes.

qa.q: In which direction does an impulse travel through a neuron?
qa.e: Dendrites pick up the information, it passes through the cell body and travels along the axon to its end.

qa.q: What is a synapse?
qa.a: The gap between the end of one neuron and the next cell
qa.e: At the synapse, chemicals released from the axon end carry the message across to the next neuron or a muscle.

qa.q: Where are reflex arcs mostly formed?
qa.e: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord so the response is quick, though the brain also receives the information.

qa.q: Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions like salivation and vomiting?
qa.e: The medulla in the hindbrain controls such involuntary actions, along with blood pressure.

qa.q: Picking up a pencil accurately depends mainly on the —
qa.e: The cerebellum makes voluntary actions precise and helps maintain posture and balance.

qa.q: How do muscle cells shorten when they receive a nerve impulse?
qa.a: Special proteins in them change shape and arrangement
qa.e: Muscle cells contain proteins that change their shape and arrangement, making the cell shorter.

qa.q: Which part of the neuron acquires information from the surroundings?
qa.e: Dendrite tips pick up information and set off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse.

qa.q: How is the brain protected inside the body?
qa.a: By the skull and a fluid-filled cushion around it
qa.e: The brain sits in the bony skull, cushioned by fluid that absorbs shocks.

qa.q: Which hormone prepares the body to face an emergency?
qa.e: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands speeds up heartbeat and breathing and diverts blood to muscles.

qa.q: Which mineral is needed by the thyroid gland to make thyroxine?
qa.e: Thyroxine contains iodine, so iodine deficiency can cause goitre.

qa.q: A person whose pancreas produces too little insulin is likely to have —
qa.e: Insulin regulates blood sugar; too little insulin raises blood sugar, causing diabetes.

qa.q: Which gland secretes growth hormone?
qa.e: The pituitary gland secretes growth hormone, controlled by a releasing factor from the hypothalamus.

qa.q: How do hormones reach their target organs?
qa.e: Endocrine glands have no ducts; hormones are released directly into blood, which carries them around the body.

qa.q: Which hormone is responsible for changes in boys at puberty, like a deeper voice?
qa.e: Testosterone from the testes brings about male puberty changes.

qa.q: Which is an example of a feedback mechanism?
qa.a: Rising blood sugar causing more insulin to be released
qa.e: The result (high sugar) controls the release of insulin, which in turn brings the sugar down.

qa.q: What is the job of the hypothalamus in growth?
qa.a: It releases a factor that stimulates the pituitary to secrete growth hormone
qa.e: The hypothalamus sends a releasing factor to the pituitary, which then releases growth hormone.

qa.q: How do the leaves of the touch-me-not plant fold when touched?
qa.a: By changing the amount of water in their cells
qa.e: Cells change shape by gaining or losing water; no growth is involved, which is why the movement is quick.

qa.q: The growth of a pollen tube towards the ovule is an example of —
qa.e: The pollen tube grows in response to chemicals released near the ovule.

qa.q: Why does a shoot bend towards light coming from one side?
qa.a: Auxin collects on the shaded side, making those cells grow longer
qa.e: More auxin on the shady side causes more elongation there, so the shoot curves towards light.

qa.q: Which plant hormone inhibits growth?
qa.e: Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves; the other three promote growth.

qa.q: Roots grow towards the earth. This is —
qa.e: Growth in the direction of gravity is positive geotropism.

qa.q: How does a pea tendril wind around a support?
qa.a: The part away from the support grows faster
qa.e: Faster growth on the outer side (away from the support) makes the tendril coil around it.

qa.q: Cytokinins are present in high concentration in —
qa.a: Areas of rapid cell division such as fruits and seeds
qa.e: Cytokinins promote cell division and are found where cells divide rapidly.

qa.q: Which is the main difference between control in plants and in animals?
qa.a: Plants use hormones and changes in cell water content, not nerves and muscles
qa.e: Plants lack nervous tissue and muscles; they coordinate through plant hormones and cell changes.

qa.q: Why are small variations produced during reproduction?
qa.a: DNA copying is not perfectly accurate
qa.e: No copying process is perfect; small changes in DNA copies lead to variation.

qa.q: Which organism reproduces by multiple fission?
qa.e: Plasmodium, the malaria parasite, divides into many daughter cells at once.

qa.q: Hydra reproduces by —
qa.e: Hydra forms buds from regenerative cells, and it can also regenerate from pieces.

qa.q: Bread mould (Rhizopus) reproduces by —
qa.e: Sporangia on its hyphae release thick-walled spores that grow on moist surfaces.

qa.q: Which plant has lost the capacity to produce seeds and is grown by vegetative propagation?
qa.e: Banana (like orange, rose and jasmine) is propagated vegetatively because it has lost the ability to produce seeds.

qa.q: Leaves of Bryophyllum can produce new plants because —
qa.a: They have buds in the notches along their margins
qa.e: Buds in the leaf notches fall on soil and grow into new plants.

qa.q: Which is an advantage of vegetative propagation?
qa.a: Plants bear flowers and fruits earlier than those grown from seeds
qa.e: Vegetatively propagated plants flower and fruit sooner and keep the parent's features.

qa.q: Leishmania differs from Amoeba in binary fission because —
qa.a: Leishmania splits in a definite plane related to its whip-like structure
qa.e: Amoeba can split in any plane, but Leishmania splits in a definite orientation.

qa.q: Which is the female reproductive part of a flower?
qa.e: The pistil (carpel) — stigma, style and ovary — is the female part.

qa.q: Which of these has unisexual flowers?
qa.e: Papaya (and watermelon) flowers have either stamens or pistil, not both.

qa.q: After fertilisation, the ovary develops into the —
qa.e: The ovary ripens into the fruit, while ovules become seeds.

qa.q: What is pollination?
qa.a: Transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma
qa.e: Pollination is only the transfer of pollen; fertilisation happens later in the ovule.

qa.q: Which part of the seed grows into the future shoot?
qa.e: The plumule becomes the shoot; the radicle becomes the root; cotyledons store food.

qa.q: Why do germ cells carry only half the amount of DNA of other body cells?
qa.a: So that the zygote formed by fusion has the normal amount of DNA
qa.e: If germ cells had full DNA, it would double every generation. Halving keeps the amount constant.

qa.q: Cross-pollination means pollen is transferred —
qa.a: From one flower to the stigma of another flower
qa.e: In cross-pollination, pollen reaches the stigma of a different flower, often by wind, water or animals.

qa.q: Where does fertilisation take place in a flowering plant?
qa.a: In the ovule inside the ovary
qa.e: The pollen tube carries the male germ cell through the style to the ovule, where it fuses with the egg.

qa.q: Why are the testes located outside the abdominal cavity?
qa.a: Because sperm formation needs a temperature lower than body temperature
qa.e: Sperm are formed best at a slightly lower temperature, which the scrotum provides.

qa.q: Where does fertilisation normally take place in the human female?
qa.e: The egg is fertilised in the oviduct; the embryo then moves to the uterus and implants.

qa.q: What is the function of the placenta?
qa.a: To provide nutrition and oxygen to the embryo from the mother's blood and remove its wastes
qa.e: The placenta has villi on the embryo's side that exchange glucose, oxygen and wastes with the mother's blood.

qa.q: Menstruation occurs when —
qa.a: The egg is not fertilised and the uterus lining breaks down
qa.e: Without fertilisation, the thick uterine lining is not needed, so it breaks down and comes out.

qa.q: Which disease is caused by a virus and can spread through sexual contact?
qa.e: HIV-AIDS (and warts) are viral; gonorrhoea and syphilis are bacterial.

qa.q: Which contraceptive method also helps prevent the spread of sexually transmitted infections?
qa.e: A condom is a physical barrier, so it reduces infection spread as well as preventing pregnancy.

qa.q: In a vasectomy, which part is blocked?
qa.e: Vasectomy blocks the vas deferens so sperm cannot be transferred; tubectomy blocks the fallopian tubes.

qa.q: Which statement about prenatal sex determination in India is correct?
qa.a: It is banned by law, to prevent sex selection
qa.e: Indian law bans finding out or revealing a baby's sex before birth, to prevent sex selection, protect the girl child and keep a healthy sex ratio.

qa.q: In Mendel's cross TT × tt, what are the F1 plants?
qa.e: All F1 plants are Tt; tall is dominant, so all are tall.

qa.q: What is the phenotypic ratio of tall to short plants in Mendel's F2 monohybrid cross?
qa.e: Tt × Tt gives 3 tall (TT, Tt, Tt) to 1 short (tt).

qa.q: In F2, about 400 plants were raised from F1 tall plants. How many would you expect to be short?
qa.e: One in four F2 plants is tt (short): 400 ÷ 4 = 100.

qa.q: Which trait is recessive in pea plants?
qa.e: Short height is recessive; it appears only in tt plants.

qa.q: What is the genotype ratio TT : Tt : tt in the F2 generation?
qa.e: Tt × Tt gives one TT, two Tt and one tt.

qa.q: A pea plant is tall. Its genotype could be —
qa.e: One dominant allele is enough for tallness, so a tall plant may be TT or Tt.

qa.q: Why did the short trait reappear in F2 although all F1 plants were tall?
qa.a: F1 plants carried the hidden short factor (t), and two t's came together in some F2 plants
qa.e: The recessive factor was present but masked in F1; tt combinations appear in F2.

qa.q: Mendel's 'factors' are today called —
qa.e: The units controlling traits are genes, which are sections of DNA on chromosomes.

qa.q: What does a gene directly control?
qa.a: The making of a specific protein
qa.e: A gene is a section of DNA that provides the information for making a protein, which then affects a trait.

qa.q: In Mendel's dihybrid cross, what was the F1 generation?
qa.e: Round and yellow are dominant, so all RrYy F1 plants show round yellow seeds.

qa.q: In a dihybrid F2 generation of 160 plants, how many are expected to have round yellow seeds?
qa.e: Round yellow is 9 out of 16 parts: 160 × 9/16 = 90.

qa.q: The appearance of new combinations like round green seeds in F2 shows that —
qa.a: Traits are inherited independently of each other
qa.e: Seed shape and seed colour were sorted separately, giving new combinations.

qa.q: How many copies of each gene does a normal body cell have?
qa.e: One copy comes from each parent, so a body cell has two.

qa.q: Why do germ cells contain only one set of chromosomes?
qa.a: So the offspring has the right number after two germ cells fuse
qa.e: Two half-sets combine at fertilisation to restore the full number of chromosomes.

qa.q: A tall plant has more of a certain plant hormone. How is this linked to its gene?
qa.a: The gene makes an efficient enzyme, which produces more hormone and makes the plant taller
qa.e: Genes code for proteins such as enzymes; an efficient enzyme makes more hormone, affecting height.

qa.q: Which statement about inheritance in humans is correct?
qa.a: Both parents contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material
qa.e: Each parent contributes one copy of every gene, i.e. almost equal genetic material.

qa.q: How many pairs of chromosomes are there in a human body cell?
qa.e: There are 23 pairs (46 chromosomes): 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes.

qa.q: What are the sex chromosomes of a human male?
qa.e: Males have one X and one Y chromosome.

qa.q: Which parent's chromosome decides the sex of a child?
qa.a: Father's, because sperm carry either X or Y
qa.e: All eggs carry X; it is the sperm (X or Y) that decides the child's sex.

qa.q: What is the probability that a child will be a girl?
qa.e: Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y, so the chance is 1/2 each time.

qa.q: In some reptiles, the sex of the young is decided by —
qa.a: The temperature at which the fertilised eggs are kept
qa.e: In some reptiles, incubation temperature determines the sex of the offspring.

qa.q: A sperm carrying a Y chromosome fertilises an egg. The baby will be —
qa.e: The egg gives X and the sperm gives Y, making XY — a boy.

qa.q: How many autosome pairs does a human have?
qa.e: Out of 23 pairs, 22 pairs are autosomes and 1 pair are sex chromosomes.

qa.q: Which statement is correct?
qa.a: All eggs carry the X chromosome
qa.e: Eggs always carry X. The Y chromosome is shorter than X, and females are XX.

qa.q: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
qa.e: By the first law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

qa.q: The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is 24 cm. What is its focal length?
Which mirror is called a diverging mirror?
qa.e: A convex mirror spreads out parallel rays, which appear to come from its focus behind the mirror.

qa.q: The focus of a concave mirror lies —
qa.a: Midway between the pole and the centre of curvature
qa.e: Since R = 2f, F is halfway between P and C, in front of the mirror.

qa.q: Why is 'AMBULANCE' written in reverse on the front of ambulances?
qa.a: So that drivers ahead read it correctly in their rear-view mirrors, which laterally invert it
qa.e: Mirrors laterally invert images, so reversed writing appears correct in the mirror.

qa.q: The line passing through the pole and the centre of curvature of a mirror is called the —
qa.e: That line is the principal axis; it is normal to the mirror at the pole.

qa.q: Which statement about a plane mirror image is correct?
qa.a: It is virtual, erect and of the same size as the object
qa.e: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-sized image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

qa.q: The focal length of a spherical mirror is 20 cm. What is its radius of curvature?
An object is placed at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. The image is —
qa.a: At C, real, inverted and the same size
qa.e: For an object at C, the reflected rays meet at C, giving a real, inverted image of the same size.

qa.q: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles, and why?
qa.a: Convex, because it gives an erect, diminished image and a wider field of view
qa.e: A convex mirror always gives an erect image and lets the driver see a large area behind.

qa.q: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. What is the image distance v (with sign)?
qa.e: Positive v means the image is behind the mirror, as expected for a convex mirror.

qa.q: A concave mirror forms an image at v = −30 cm of an object at u = −10 cm. What is the magnification?
qa.e: m = −v/u = −(−30)/(−10) = −3. Negative m means the image is real and inverted, and it is 3 times the size of the object.

qa.q: Where should an object be placed in front of a concave mirror to get a virtual, erect and enlarged image?
qa.e: Only when the object is between the pole and the focus does a concave mirror give a virtual, erect, enlarged image — as in a shaving mirror.

qa.q: In the New Cartesian sign convention, the focal length of a concave mirror is taken as —
qa.e: The focus of a concave mirror lies in front of it, against the direction of incident light, so f is negative.

qa.q: Solving the mirror formula, the magnification of an image comes out as −0.5. The image is —
qa.e: Negative m means real and inverted; |m| = 0.5 < 1 means diminished.

qa.q: Why is a concave mirror used by dentists?
qa.a: When held close, it gives an enlarged, erect image of the teeth
qa.e: With the tooth between P and F, a concave mirror forms an enlarged, virtual, erect image.

qa.q: Why does light bend when it passes obliquely from air into water?
qa.e: Light travels more slowly in water than in air; this change in speed causes bending.

qa.q: The refractive index of a glass is 1.5. What is the speed of light in it, in units of 10⁸ m/s?
Which medium in this list is optically densest?
qa.e: The higher the refractive index, the optically denser the medium and the slower light travels in it.

qa.q: A ray of light passes from glass into air. It bends —
qa.e: Going from denser to rarer, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

qa.q: What does Snell's law state?
qa.a: sin i / sin r is a constant for a given pair of media
qa.e: For a given colour of light and pair of media, the ratio sin i/sin r is constant — the refractive index.

qa.q: Kerosene floats on water, yet it has a higher refractive index. What does this tell us?
qa.a: Optical density is different from mass density
qa.e: Optical density relates to the speed of light in a medium, not to mass per unit volume.

qa.q: Light travels in medium 1 at 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s and in medium 2 at 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1?
When light passes through a rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is —
qa.a: Parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced
qa.e: The bending at the two parallel faces is equal and opposite, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.

qa.q: An object is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. What is the image distance v (with sign)?
qa.e: v = +30 cm, so a real image forms on the other side of the lens.

qa.q: In the same case (u = −15 cm, v = +30 cm), what is the magnification?
qa.e: m = v/u = 30 ÷ (−15) = −2: a real, inverted image twice as tall.

qa.q: What is the power of a convex lens of focal length 25 cm, in dioptres?
qa.e: P = 1/f with f in metres: 1 ÷ 0.25 = +4 D.

qa.q: A concave lens has a focal length of 50 cm. What is its power, in dioptres?
qa.e: f = −0.5 m for a concave lens, so P = 1 ÷ (−0.5) = −2 D.

qa.q: Where must an object be placed in front of a convex lens to get an image of the same size?
qa.e: With the object at 2F₁, a real, inverted image of the same size forms at 2F₂.

qa.q: A concave lens always forms an image that is —
qa.e: Whatever the object's position, a concave lens gives a virtual, erect, diminished image.

qa.q: A lens has a power of −2.5 D. What type of lens is it?
qa.e: Negative power means negative focal length, which is a concave (diverging) lens.

qa.q: Two thin lenses of power +2.0 D and −0.5 D are placed in contact. What is the combined power, in dioptres?
What is the near point of a young adult with normal vision?
qa.e: The least distance of distinct vision for a normal young eye is about 25 cm.

qa.q: Which part of the eye does most of the refraction of light?
qa.e: Most refraction happens at the outer surface of the cornea; the lens only fine-tunes the focus.

qa.q: When we look at a distant tree, the ciliary muscles —
qa.e: Relaxed ciliary muscles let the lens become thin, increasing its focal length for distant objects.

qa.q: A person cannot see distant objects clearly. Which lens corrects this defect?
qa.e: This is myopia; a concave (diverging) lens moves the image back onto the retina.

qa.q: A myopic person's far point is 2 m. What is the power of the correcting lens, in dioptres?
qa.e: f = −2 m (concave), so P = 1/f = −0.5 D.

qa.q: Which is a cause of hypermetropia?
qa.a: The eyeball has become too small
qa.e: A short eyeball (or a lens with too long a focal length) makes light focus behind the retina.

qa.q: Why do many elderly people need reading glasses?
qa.a: Presbyopia: ciliary muscles weaken and the lens becomes less flexible
qa.e: With age the power of accommodation decreases, so the near point moves farther away.

qa.q: What happens in cataract?
qa.a: The crystalline lens becomes milky and cloudy
qa.e: A cloudy lens blocks light, causing partial or total loss of vision; surgery can restore sight.

qa.q: What is the splitting of white light into its component colours called?
qa.e: Dispersion happens because different colours bend by different amounts.

qa.q: Which colour of light bends the most when passing through a prism?
qa.e: Violet is deviated most and red least.

qa.q: Why does a prism split white light into colours?
qa.a: Each colour bends through a different angle
qa.e: The refractive index of glass is slightly different for each colour, so each is deviated by a different amount.

qa.q: Who first used a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight?
qa.e: Isaac Newton obtained the spectrum and recombined it with a second inverted prism.

qa.q: Which processes in water droplets form a rainbow?
qa.a: Refraction and dispersion, internal reflection, then refraction again
qa.e: Sunlight is refracted and dispersed entering a droplet, reflected inside, and refracted again as it leaves.

qa.q: The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray in a prism is called the —
qa.e: It measures how much the prism has turned the ray from its original path.

qa.q: In which direction must you look to see a rainbow?
qa.a: Away from the Sun, with the Sun behind you
qa.e: Light comes back from droplets in front of you only if the Sun is behind you.

qa.q: How many colours are usually listed in the spectrum of white light?
qa.e: VIBGYOR: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red — seven colours.

qa.q: Why does the clear sky look blue?
qa.a: Air molecules scatter blue light more than red light
qa.e: Molecules smaller than the wavelength of visible light scatter shorter wavelengths (blue) much more strongly.

qa.q: Sunlight passing through gaps in a forest canopy shows visible beams. This is due to —
qa.e: Tiny water droplets and dust in the air scatter the light, making the beam's path visible.

qa.q: Why are danger signals red in colour?
qa.a: Red light is scattered the least by fog and smoke
qa.e: Being least scattered, red light reaches far through fog or smoke.

qa.q: What would the sky look like to an astronaut far above the atmosphere?
qa.e: With no air to scatter sunlight, the sky appears dark.

qa.q: Very large particles in the air scatter light so that it appears —
qa.e: When particles are large enough, all colours are scattered about equally, so the light looks white.

qa.q: The wavelength of red light is about how many times that of blue light?
qa.e: Red light's wavelength is about 1.8 times that of blue light, so it is scattered much less.

qa.q: The colour of scattered light depends mainly on —
qa.a: The size of the scattering particles
qa.e: Fine particles scatter blue; larger ones scatter longer wavelengths; very large ones scatter all colours.

qa.q: Which is an example of the Tyndall effect?
qa.a: A beam of light visible in a smoke-filled room
qa.e: Smoke particles scatter light, making the beam's path visible.

qa.q: A current of 0.5 A flows through a lamp for 10 minutes. How much charge (in coulombs) flows?
How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?
qa.e: An ammeter measures the current flowing through a component, so it is placed in series.

qa.q: How much work (in joules) is done in moving a charge of 2 C across a potential difference of 12 V?
What is the resistance (in ohms) of a bulb filament that draws 0.5 A from a 220 V supply?
A wire's length is doubled while its thickness and material stay the same. Its resistance —
qa.e: R = ρl/A, so R is directly proportional to length.

qa.q: Why are heating elements made of alloys such as nichrome?
qa.a: They have high resistivity and do not oxidise readily at high temperatures
qa.e: A high resistivity alloy produces more heat and does not burn (oxidise) easily when red hot.

qa.q: Ohm's law is valid only when —
qa.a: The temperature of the conductor remains constant
qa.e: Resistance changes with temperature, so V ∝ I holds only at constant temperature.

qa.q: Two wires of the same material and length have cross-sectional areas A and 2A. Compared with the thin wire, the thick wire's resistance is —
qa.e: R = ρl/A, so doubling the area halves the resistance.

qa.q: Resistors of 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 15 Ω are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
qa.e: In series, resistances simply add: 5 + 10 + 15 = 30 Ω.

qa.q: Resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
Three resistors of 6 Ω each are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
A 12 V battery is connected to 2 Ω and 4 Ω resistors in series. What current (in amperes) flows?
In the same series circuit (2 Ω and 4 Ω, 12 V, 2 A), what is the potential difference (in volts) across the 4 Ω resistor?
qa.e: V = IR = 2 × 4 = 8 V. The remaining 4 V is across the 2 Ω resistor.

qa.q: Why are household appliances connected in parallel?
qa.a: So each gets the full voltage and can be switched on or off independently
qa.e: Parallel connection gives each appliance the mains voltage and its own current path.

qa.q: When more resistors are added in parallel, the equivalent resistance —
qa.e: Each new branch gives charge another path, so total resistance falls.

qa.q: Two 10 Ω resistors are connected in parallel across a 5 V cell. What is the current (in amperes) through each resistor?
qa.e: Each resistor has 5 V across it: I = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 A. Total current is 1 A.

qa.q: A current of 2 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor for 30 s. How much heat (in joules) is produced?
What is the power (in watts) of an appliance that draws 5 A from a 220 V supply?
A 1000 W heater is used for 2 hours a day. How many units (kWh) does it use per day?
qa.e: Energy = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh.

qa.q: If the cost of electricity is ₹6 per unit, what is the cost of using 2 units?
Why are bulbs filled with nitrogen and argon?
qa.a: These chemically inactive gases prolong the life of the filament
qa.e: Inert gases prevent the hot filament from reacting with oxygen and burning out quickly.

qa.q: How is a fuse connected in a circuit, and why?
qa.a: In series, so it can break the whole circuit when the current is too large
qa.e: All the current must pass through the fuse; if it melts, the circuit breaks.

qa.q: A bulb rated 100 W, 220 V. What is its resistance, in ohms?
How many joules are there in 1 kWh?
Who discovered that an electric current deflects a nearby compass needle?
qa.e: Oersted observed this in 1820, linking electricity and magnetism.

qa.q: Why do two magnetic field lines never intersect?
qa.a: Because a compass at the crossing would point in two directions at once
qa.e: The field has only one direction at any point, so lines cannot cross.

qa.q: Inside a bar magnet, the field lines run —
qa.e: Field lines are closed curves: N → S outside and S → N inside.

qa.q: What is the pattern of the magnetic field around a straight wire carrying current?
qa.a: Concentric circles centred on the wire
qa.e: The field lines form circles around the wire in planes perpendicular to it.

qa.q: What happens to the magnetic field at a point near a straight wire if the current is increased?
qa.e: The field strength is directly related to the current.

qa.q: The right-hand thumb rule gives the —
qa.a: Direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire
qa.e: With the thumb along the current, curled fingers show the field's direction.

qa.q: A coil of 50 turns is replaced by one of 100 turns carrying the same current. The field at its centre —
qa.e: Each turn adds its field, so doubling the turns about doubles the field.

qa.q: The magnetic field near a current-carrying straight wire is weaker —
qa.e: The field decreases as the distance from the wire increases.

qa.q: The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is —
qa.e: Inside a solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, showing a uniform field.

qa.q: Which material is best for the core of an electromagnet?
qa.e: Soft iron becomes strongly magnetised when current flows and loses magnetism when it stops.

qa.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the forefinger shows the direction of —
qa.e: Forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = force or motion.

qa.q: When is the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field the greatest?
qa.a: When the current is perpendicular to the field
qa.e: The force is maximum when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.

qa.q: What happens to the force on a conductor if the direction of current is reversed?
qa.e: Reversing either the current or the field reverses the direction of the force.

qa.q: The field pattern of a current-carrying solenoid is similar to that of —
qa.e: One end of the solenoid acts as a north pole, the other as a south pole, just like a bar magnet.

qa.q: Which change makes an electromagnet stronger?
qa.e: More current or more turns gives a stronger magnetic field.

qa.q: A scientist who suggested that a magnet also experiences an equal and opposite force from a current-carrying conductor was —
qa.e: Ampère suggested that since a current exerts a force on a magnet, the magnet must exert an equal and opposite force on the conductor.

qa.q: What is the frequency of AC supply in India, in hertz?
qa.e: Indian mains AC has a frequency of 50 Hz.

qa.q: What is the potential difference between the live and neutral wires in Indian homes, in volts?
qa.e: In India the mains supply is at 220 V.

qa.q: What colour is the insulation of the earth wire?
qa.e: Live is red, neutral is black and earth is green.

qa.q: Why is the earth wire connected to the metal body of an appliance?
qa.a: To provide a low-resistance path for leaking current, preventing a severe shock
qa.e: Any leakage current flows to earth instead of through the person touching the appliance.

qa.q: What is short-circuiting?
qa.a: When the live wire and neutral wire come into direct contact
qa.e: Direct contact lowers resistance sharply, so the current rises abruptly and the fuse should blow.

qa.q: Which is an advantage of AC over DC?
qa.a: AC can be transmitted over long distances without much loss of energy
qa.e: That is why power stations send AC to our homes.

qa.q: Which appliance should be on the 15 A circuit?
qa.e: High-power appliances like geysers draw large currents and use the 15 A circuit.

qa.q: Overloading of a household circuit can happen when —
qa.a: Too many appliances are connected to a single socket
qa.e: Too many appliances draw too much current; an accidental rise in supply voltage can also overload a circuit.

qa.q: Which of these is an artificial ecosystem?
qa.e: Crop fields, gardens and aquariums are made and maintained by humans.

qa.q: Grass → deer → lion. At which trophic level is the lion?
qa.e: Grass (producer) is first, deer (herbivore) second and lion (carnivore) third.

qa.q: According to the 10 percent law, if producers have 10,000 J of energy, how much (in joules) reaches the primary consumers?
qa.e: About 10% of 10,000 J = 1000 J is passed on to the herbivores.

qa.q: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?
qa.a: They break down dead remains and return nutrients to the soil
qa.e: Bacteria and fungi break complex organic matter into simple substances that plants reuse.

qa.q: Why are food chains generally limited to three or four steps?
qa.a: So much energy is lost at each level that little is left for higher levels
qa.e: Only about 10% of energy passes on each time, so after a few steps too little remains to support another level.

qa.q: About what percentage of the sunlight falling on leaves do green plants capture?
qa.e: Green plants convert about 1% of the sunlight falling on their leaves into food energy.

qa.q: Why is the flow of energy in an ecosystem called unidirectional?
qa.a: Energy moves from plants to herbivores to carnivores and never returns to the previous level
qa.e: Energy captured by producers moves up the levels and is not passed back; nutrients, unlike energy, are recycled by decomposers.

qa.q: Which is an abiotic component of an ecosystem?
qa.e: Abiotic factors are non-living: temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals.

qa.q: What is the chemical formula of ozone?
qa.e: Ozone has three oxygen atoms in each molecule.

qa.q: What does the ozone layer protect us from?
qa.e: Ozone shields the Earth's surface from harmful UV radiation, which can cause skin cancer.

qa.q: Which chemicals are mainly linked to the depletion of the ozone layer?
qa.e: CFCs, used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers, damage the ozone layer.

qa.q: Which reaction shows ozone forming in the upper atmosphere?
qa.e: UV splits O₂ into free oxygen atoms; each atom combines with O₂ to form O₃.

qa.q: In which year did UNEP succeed in forging an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels?
qa.e: The agreement was reached in 1987.

qa.q: Ozone near the ground is —
qa.e: Ozone is protective in the upper atmosphere but poisonous at ground level.

qa.q: When did the amount of ozone in the atmosphere begin to drop sharply?
qa.e: Scientists noticed the sharp drop in the 1980s and linked it to CFCs.

qa.q: Which step helps protect the ozone layer?
qa.e: Avoiding CFCs reduces ozone depletion; CFC-free refrigerators are now mandatory worldwide.

qa.q: Which of these is non-biodegradable?
qa.e: Polythene is not broken down by bacteria or fungi and persists in the environment.

qa.q: What is biological magnification?
qa.a: Increase in concentration of harmful non-biodegradable chemicals at successive trophic levels
qa.e: Chemicals that are not broken down accumulate as they pass up the food chain.

qa.q: In the food chain plankton → small fish → large fish → fish-eating bird, where will a non-biodegradable pesticide be most concentrated?
qa.e: It accumulates at each level, so the top consumer has the highest concentration.

qa.q: Why are biodegradable substances less harmful to the environment?
qa.a: They are broken down by bacteria and fungi into simpler substances
qa.e: Decomposers break them down, returning nutrients to the soil instead of piling up.

qa.q: Which is the best first step for managing waste at home?
qa.e: Segregation lets wet waste be composted and dry waste be recycled.

qa.q: Which agents break down biodegradable waste?
qa.e: Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break down organic matter.

qa.q: Why do humans often have high levels of some pesticides in their bodies?
qa.a: Humans are at the top of many food chains, where these chemicals accumulate
qa.e: Being top consumers, humans receive chemicals that have built up through all lower levels.

qa.q: Which action reduces non-biodegradable waste?
qa.a: Using a cloth bag for shopping
qa.e: Reusable cloth bags reduce the use of polythene bags.
